articles.title: Ralph Fiennes Had A Sick Robert Pattinson Burn When Asked Who Could Take Over For Voldemort
articles.summary: Even the original Dark Lord himself has the Pattinson Jokes.
articles.content:
Robert Pattinson was just announced as the next James Bond , and the internet has spent the days since joking that no Hollywood role is safe from him. I thought those jokes had about run their course until Ralph Fiennes weighed in. The actor who terrified an entire generation of Harry Potter fans as Lord Voldemort was asked who should take over the role in HBO's upcoming television series, and his answer was so dry that I almost missed how funny it was.

I love how little effort went into that joke. The Red Dragon veteran actor didn't need to explain it, either. Following Pattinson's Bond casting, social media has been having a field day with the idea that he's taking every acting job . One popular variation suggests that artificial intelligence isn't coming for anyone's job because Pattinson will get there first. The OG Potter villain apparently decided to throw one more highly coveted part onto the pile.

The two actors also have a second franchise connection thanks to Bond. Fiennes played M opposite Daniel Craig in Skyfall , Spectre and No Time to Die , so he's watched a different actor occupy the 007 role that Pattinson is now inheriting. The Tenet actor has already spent plenty of time bouncing between massive franchises, from Twilight to The Batman . It's getting hard to name an iconic fictional universe he hasn't visited.

From filmmakers Greg Yagolnitzer and Raviv Ullman, "Drag" centers on two sisters who don't get along and who set out to burgle a remote house in upstate New York. The job goes wrong fast. One sister puts her back out and can't move from the upper floor, and the pair must find a way out before the owner gets home. Lucy DeVito and Christine Ko round out the cast.

Danny, Lucy and Jake DeVito produced through Jersey Films 2nd Avenue, the production company they founded, and the film is the company's first independent feature. articles.title: British Industry Braces For Impact Of America's Federal Film & TV Tax Incentive
articles.summary: EXCLUSIVE: Steven Paul may think the proposed federal film and TV tax incentive is "good for the world," but the British industry isn't so sure. UK trade bodies, industry organizations and studios are peering nervously toward the other side of the pond at the incentive's progress, which has now received the full-throated backing of Donald […]
articles.content:
EXCLUSIVE: Steven Paul may think the proposed federal film and TV tax incentive is "good for the world," but the British industry isn't so sure.

UK trade bodies, industry organizations and studios are peering nervously toward the other side of the pond at the incentive's progress, which has now received the full-throated backing of Donald Trump. That is because American studios and streamers have made huge productions in the UK for years including the likes of Barbie, Wicked and Amazon's Lord of the Rings, generating billions in local production revenue and creating tens of thousands of jobs. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article1-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid","mid-articleX","mid-article","300x251"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[2,2],[300,250],[620,350],[300,251],[501,282],[3,3],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366]]) .exemptFromSleep() .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories News UK Culture Minister Delivers Emotional Plea To YouTube To "Set An Example" & Remove Russell Brand's Channel News BFI & Chanel Filmmaker Award: 'Ish' Director Imran Perretta Among 2026 Winners

Deadline understands the British Film Institute ( BFI ) has formed a working group with other industry bodies and bigwigs to probe the incentive's potential impact on the sector and consider what levers can be pulled to nullify this impact. Watch on Deadline if ( !window.pmc.harmony?.isEventAdScheduledTime() ) { pmcCnx.cmd.push(function() { pmcCnx({ settings: { plugins: { pmcAtlasMG: { iabPlcmt: 2, } } }, playerId: '32fe25c4-79aa-406a-af44-69b41e969e71', playlistId: '0199e506-e642-7728-8264-463efe71337b', }).render("connatix_contextual_player_div"); }); } else { // This should only be get called when page cache is not cleared and it's event time. window.pmc.harmony?.switchToHarmonyPlayer(); }

The working group was assembled recently and is not only tackling the tax incentive but wider macro issues hitting the film and TV industry such as the slowdown in commissioning, falling budgets, job cuts and sharper competition from tax credits in other nations and U.S. states. "A broad group of screen sector organisations have come together to identify measures which will ensure the UK remains a world-leading home for domestic and international production," said a BFI spokeswoman. "This is looking at a range of challenging conditions facing the sector, including increased international competitiveness.”

The fear is that the attractiveness of the proposed 20% American credit — Trump has urged lawmakers to pass the "amazing" bipartisan bill — and broader drive to bring production back to the U.S. will make studios think twice before setting up projects in the UK. While there is clearly political will in the U.S. to force the measure through after years of losing local production, possibly before the current lame-duck congress session concludes, UK industry sources cautioned that there is no sign of productions relocating today. Big projects filming in Q4 2026 and next year include new seasons of Mobland and House of the Dragon , along with Guy Ritchie's Dogfight for Netflix. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dl-mid-article-inject2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article2","mid-articleX","mid-article","mid","300x251"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366]]) .exemptFromSleep() .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Potential levers could include improving the UK's own 25% tax credit, generating more funding from elsewhere or improving local production. Improving the UK tax credit, which has been a huge success story since coming in more than a decade ago, has been discussed for many years but the ruling Labour Party has shown little inclination to play ball .

"There are levers and we need to discuss them," said one industry source familar with the working group. "This isn't just about raising [our own] tax credits. We need to improve the domestic situation."

The UK government has now weighed in publicly.

In what felt a deliberate and timely intervention, culture minister Ian Murray told last week's British Screen Forum conference his team "takes the implications [of the credit] incredibly seriously." Without elaborating, Murray said the outcome "remains to be seen."

Murray's team declined further comment on what actions the government is taking but sources have welcomed his remarks as proof the government is cognisant of the issue. "Ian was showing the industry he has their back," said the industry source quoted above.

At the same event, Aardman boss Sean Clarke described the tax credit as a "real issue" for the industry. This is because inward investment, most of it from Americans, has for years made up the bulk of Britain's film and TV revenue. But amid a worldwide commissioning slowdown, this has been slipping. Recent BFI figures showed that spend on film and high-end TV plummeted by 28% for the year to September 30. The figures are "the result of a complex picture, ranging from significant shifts in the global industrial context through to increased competitiveness from other international territories, and set against a backdrop of a strong Q1-Q3 period in 2025," the BFI spokeswoman said, pointing to huge projects that filmed in 2025 like Avengers: Doomsday , Spider-Man: Brand New Day and the Harry Potter TV series.

The UK, with its lucrative credit and envious skills base, no doubt remains an enormous production hub, and no one thinks this will suddenly screech to a halt. But with all these headwinds already being navigated, any further disruption would be most unwelcome.

Paul flew the flag for the incentive during a fireside chat at Qatar Film Committee’s Industry Days event in Doha earlier last week, claiming it will be "good for the world." The Hollywood veteran may find it tough to convince Brits of his way of thinking.

articles.content:
"I loved your script. It is perfect. Now change everything."

While probably far from a joke for many screenwriters who have had similar conversations, this particular line is taken from upcoming satirical picture book "We Make a Movie."

Designed to look like a children's book from the 1960s (particularly the U.K.'s famed "Key Words" educational series by Ladybird), "We Make a Movie" comes from artist Miriam Elia and film industry analyst Stephen Follows and features 20 hand-painted pictures accompanied by short, cheery lines merrily roasting Hollywood and the film industry at large. At the bottom of each are three "new words" to explain what's really going on (in the case of the script line, the words are "squash," "original" and "voices"). blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories Taylor Swift's 'Law & Order: SVU' Crime Scene Evidence Board from the Emmys Goes on Display at the Paley Center (EXCLUSIVE) TV Academy Cancels Televerse for 2027 Emmy Season; Festival Will Return in Early 2028

"The script says Paris by dawn. The tax break says Eastern Europe," reads another page likely to make more than a few producers nod knowingly. "'I loved your film,' says the sales agent. He has not seen it," adds another.

"Every page comes from something true," said Follows, who has published more than 600 data-led studies of the industry and is regularly cited in the press. "Anyone in the business will recognize it, and the people it's about will laugh along without realizing it's them."

Due out next month, "We Make a Movie" has already become something of a hit in the film industry. Pre-orders for the first edition (available to order at www.wemakeamovie.com ) are on course to sell out, with a second run being planned.

"'We Make a Movie' is the book of the year — it explains the film industry in a nutshell and in the most entertaining and funny way ever," said Uwe Boll. "I loved it! A lot of truth to it." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

articles.title: SNL Fans Just Made The Thanksgiving Comment About 'Sister' I Was Already Thinking
articles.summary: Bring on the awkward dinner table conversations.
articles.content:
I can’t remember the last time an SNL sketch went as viral as “Sister” did a week ago. While impressions, “Weekend Update” and host and musical guest moment s are topics of conversation at Studio 8h every week, everyone and their mother saw the “Sister” sketch, and now all those people are going to be in a confined space with one another over Thanksgiving weekend. The comment section is all over this awkwardness.

Written by Chase Rosenberg, Mikey Day, Streeter Seidell, and Simon Rich, the sketch follows brothers who have implemented their “sister” for elder care, and have then stepped back to let her handle everything that comes with that label. It’s really funny, but there are also many rings of truth to it, and it has sparked a lot of conversation from angry siblings who feel burnt out and tasked with doing too much. It's led to so much discourse in the days after its release, I'd imagine it will land on the list of Saturday Night Live sketches we'll talk about for years .

In fact, lots of people think the timing of the SNL sketch was perfect or awful, depending on what you think about it. I don't want to harp too hard

One viral tweet also noted the release of the sketch just before family get togethers had to be “deliberate." (Again, it's definitely interesting.)

To note, I don't personally agree with the bent that SNL deserves a bad rap. The show has had ups and downs as long as I've watched it, and silly bits can sometimes drive home harder than some of the political or Update stuff. While not on topic to Thanksgiving like the Adele-themed "Thanksgiving Miracle" sketch with Aidy Bryant, I do think this is one we will continue to watch and discuss this week.

I'd just recommend people do so before people are too hyped up on tryptophan, alcohol and sugar.

articles.title: 'The Body' Star Kristina Bogic Just Wanted to Take Care of Anya: "A Lot of Young Women Can Relate"
articles.summary: The 19-year-old star of Netflix's latest hit breaks down how she came to love her dance team captain character: "Anya always wants to try and do the right thing."
articles.content:
The Body team searched far and wide to find their leading lady, Anya. Kristina Bogic , the 19-year-old who landed the role, knew there were plenty of others trying for the part. "A lot of my friends had auditioned for Anya," she tells The Hollywood Reporter .

By the time the audition for The Body came her way, Bogic had faced her fair share of rejection, as any actor would. She'd had "hundreds and hundreds" of auditions before, so she had a feeling that there was no way it could be her. Newly 18 at the time, the actress just decided to go for it. And it worked out. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4],[300,251]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories Business Netflix Buys Radford Studio Lot for $380 Million TV Kevin Kline Boards 'The Corrections' at Netflix

Bogic did four chemistry reads with Sara Boustany, who plays Anya's best friend and secret romantic interest Elise in the series. The actress had "a bunch" of callbacks — she just kept getting more scripts. "I remember thinking even if I wasn't in this show, I would just be so excited to watch it," she says.

The raunchy psychological thriller has become an online favorite. Bogic felt protective over the character from moment one. "I can't believe I get to play Anya," the actress says. "I really just wanted to take care of her the whole time."

Anya's the captain of her Catholic high school's dance team. In addition to mass hysteria incidents, the teen's also dealing with complicated feelings for her best friend. Bogic wanted to keep the character tucked safely under her wing.

"I'm so happy I got to explore her warmth and also her dark sides as we," she says. "A lot of young women can relate to Anya."

Below, Bogic digs into finding the character, her relationship with her co-stars and what she thinks happened in that season finale. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

What was the hardest part in trying to find Anya?

I remember in the table reads, I was still trying to find the essence of her and who Anya was. We had eight weeks of dance training. I did some acting classes, and I did four hours of dialect coaching every week. These women on this set were so amazing at improv as well. They're so funny. It came to them so naturally. That's something I've never felt like I've struggled with, but on top of the accent, it was like I just wanted to feel so settled in it that I could experiment with whatever.

The moment I cracked Anya was when I had the conversation with Lisbeth at the fire pit. I remember Quinn [Shepard] saying she wants this essence of this cool girl. She's popular. She's the team captain. There's a level of dominance there, but also there's a level of softness. I think she still has this innocence of the world and this naivety to her, which I think I wanted to protect in this season. It starts getting stripped away from her, from her bad decisions. I do think Anya always wants to try and do the right thing.

Your character's relationship with Sara's character is a driving force of the show. How did you find that dynamic?

It was very easy, honestly. The first time we spoke, we had maybe 10 minutes just to chat on Zoom before we did the audition, and we just clicked. We were both equally as excited and passionate about the show, which I don't know if it's rare, but I've never had that experience with someone on set before. We were all so passionate and so excited to be there. We were so grateful and tried to take in every single moment of it. I think that also just came into our characters as well. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-thr-article-mid-articleX-uid2' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setLazyLoadMultiplier(2) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

[Anya] and Elise are cheeky. They're fun. I love that we kind of played [it] off as like, we're just girls. This is just what girls do. Girls hold each other's hands. Girls do this. We're just joking around. Then you realize there's obviously so much going on underneath. I feel like our chemistry was honestly quite instant. Even just as friends, me and her, we still talk all the time. Our cast is just very close in general.

What was your dancing like when you took this on?

I hadn't danced in five years before this. And I remember Quinn, after I did one of the chemistry reads with Sara, Quinn asked me to a one-minute improvised dance video. I remember thinking I was just going to film it quickly. I was in a hotel in Italy. I went outside and I was like, "All right, let me just see if I can throw something together. Let me move my body." I was so awkward. I felt like when a baby deer is just born or a baby horse and they're wobbling, that's how I felt. I didn't realize how important it is to know how your body moves.

What was the dance bootcamp like?

It gave me extra confidence. That's also how I found Anya, was I finally felt comfortable in my body. I knew how it moved and how it flowed. It tapped me into Anya's femininity, which she really values and uses as a form of currency in her life. We had eight weeks of this bootcamp with Ryan Heffington. He was so amazing. He was so patient with all of us. We're professional, but we're also little frat boys on set, that's how we act. We're just roughhousing all the time and constantly chatting and asking questions. It was a lot of energy, and he was just so amazing. I'm so grateful that we had him for those weeks. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-thr-article-mid-articleX-uid3' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setLazyLoadMultiplier(2) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Did most of you not have a background in dancing? Was it kind of fresh for a lot of people?

No, honestly. I walked in [and] everyone's a pro-level dancer. I walked into watching Emily Roman doing a front aerial. Everyone had a bit of background in dance, but we all caught onto it very quickly.

What was it like to work with these women

I think we were so lucky with this cast. Can you imagine just putting 12 girls in a room and saying now you all have to pretend to be friends? Not for one second did we ever feel like it was forced. I love every one of those girls to death, genuinely. It was so fun just seeing everyone take their character off the page. We were all there for each other, and everyone was so amazing. They completely made their character their own. There was not one sense of ego on set, not one sense of competition. We really all felt like it was very collaborative and very supportive. I remember telling this to someone in my life and they were like, "Oh, it's so rare that 12 girls are going to get together. I can imagine the drama." We had the least amount of drama ever. We were so chill. We literally got to hang out and play dress-up with our friends all day.

Can you walk me through where Anya's at in that first episode?

She's at a very desperate and vulnerable place. She's in fight-or-flight, and I think she also. It's a common theme for her to repress a lot of things. Whether it's her sexuality or it's what's happened with Grace, what's going on with Steven, her issues with sex. She's always repressing something.Even the way she presents herself, she's like, "If I look different, people are going to know something's wrong. I can't hang out with Elyse. She's going to know something's wrong." Everything is just pushed down and suppressed. Me and Anya relate to each other a little bit in this way of things snowball and then we just fall apart a little bit. She's just in a desperate state, honestly. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-thr-article-mid-articleX-uid4' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[300,250],[300,251],[620,350],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450],[4,4]]) .setLazyLoadMultiplier(2) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

What is that moment for Anya in the show that you find to be that moment of falling apart?

She has a little one in episode two, when she sees Grace outside the strip club. But that scene is actually so much funnier than I thought it would. I took it there because I thought it was going to be really dark and sad. I watch it and I'm laughing. They're so hysterical. It's so ridiculous and so funny. But episode eight for sure. It's the breaking point for her. Everything's just come out, at least within a circle, and she's been faced with everything. She can't push anything down anymore. Definitely episode eight.

At the end, do you think she's confessing because she's feeling guilty or do you think she's feeling like she can push off what's actually happening again?

I think this is genuinely how she's feeling. When she confesses… I think the reason why she can't admit a lot of things is because of this Catholic guilt and this shame. She always wants to do the right thing, so I think when it comes down to it — although maybe it's the wrong execution sometimes — it's almost like she had lost this innocence and this softness to her. That's really what she's asking for, she wants herself back — I want my life back. Nothing is going to be the same after this. How could it? That's really the plea that she's making, deep down, is I want my life back. I just want everything to go back to normal. I wish I could just repress this. Once Grace wakes up, she's like, "Oh my fucking God, it's coming for me. There's no outrightness anymore," and I think she just has to face what she's done.

A horror short rooted in the toll of sickle cell disease on India's tribal communities has won the inaugural WIF India x Google Flow Filmathon.

Promita Banerjee's "Sikkal," made with Google's AI creative workspace Google Flow, took the INR1.2 million ($12,500) first prize. Syam Manohar's black comedy "Kuli" placed second, earning INR800,000 ($8,300), and Nikhil Shinde's animated "Pedals of Joy" came third with INR400,000 ($4,200). Related Stories TV Academy Cancels Televerse for 2027 Emmy Season; Festival Will Return in Early 2028 Taylor Swift's 'Law & Order: SVU' Crime Scene Evidence Board from the Emmys Goes on Display at the Paley Center (EXCLUSIVE)

Women in Film India (WIF India) ran the Filmathon with Google Flow to open up AI filmmaking tools to emerging storytellers around the country. The call drew more than 850 registrations, and a seven-member jury that included directors Shakun Batra and Pan Nalin and Cannes Next head Sten Saluveer narrowed the field to five. The finalists were showcased at the International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Goa. Aamir Khan Productions CEO Aparna Purohit delivered a keynote at the event. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Goa Chief Minister Pramod Sawant attended the ceremony, where WIF India founder and CEO Guneet Monga Kapoor and filmmaker Ashutosh Gowariker joined the presenters on stage. Srishti Chaudhary's "Nazar" and Aswathi Naduthodi's "Bombay Mumbai – Vada Pav" were recognized as finalists.

articles.title: Avengers: Doomsday Needs a Good Reason to Explain These Missing X-Men Characters
articles.summary: Pretty much everyone who has been invested in Marvel movies for the past two and a half decades has a few reasons to be excited for Avengers: Doomsday. The film is bringing together members of the X-Men from the early 2000s, the Avengers from the 2010s, the New Avengers, the Fantastic Four, heroes from Wakanda, […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Pretty much everyone who has been invested in Marvel movies for the past two and a half decades has a few reasons to be excited for Avengers: Doomsday . The film is bringing together members of the X-Men from the early 2000s, the Avengers from the 2010s, the New Avengers, the Fantastic Four, heroes from Wakanda, and more, all to go up against the threat of Doctor Doom. A bunch of superheroes teaming up is expected in a movie like this but back when the cast was announced, the big surprises were the Fox X-Men since we hadn't seen most of them since 2014.

Those X-Men characters also hadn't really had a connection to the MCU to this point. Still, Avengers: Doomsday is set to feature Professor X, Magneto, Cyclops, Mystique, Nightcrawler, and Beast . We are all happy to have these characters back, but there is a glaring issue with their return, which is that the team isn't full. In fact, it's an odd selection of mutants, as you have a somewhat random assortment of X-Men and members of the Brotherhood of Mutants. The film needs to explain this in a satisfying way because no explanation would be bad and a lazy one could ruin the entire experience.

Without taking the prequels into account, there is a trilogy of X-Men movies from Fox , which is where the returning Avengers: Doomsday characters are from. However, some of the most important and recurring members of those teams are absent from this upcoming film. Halle Berry's Storm is a glaring omission, as one of the most powerful mutants in existence. The same goes for Famke Janssen's Jean Grey, Anna Paquin's Rogue, and Shawn Ashmore's Iceman. You could even extend it to include Elliot Page's Kitty Pryde, Ben Foster's Angel, and Daniel Cudmore's Colossus, just to name a few.

Avengers: Doomsday needs to come up wth a valid reason for the absence of these characters, especially for Jean Grey and Storm because they're such pivotal parts of the entire franchise. A simple mention that says they died or something along those lines would be awful. These are characters who deserve to have some care put into everything about them. Berry has said that she's sad she's not included, while Janssen also expressed disappointment with the MCU for leaving her out. Although Storm, Jean, and Rogue are part of the upcoming X-Men reboot, so are Magneto, Professor X, and Cyclops, and they're included.

The trailers for Avengers: Doomsday do seem to suggest that things don't go well for the X-Men. It looks like an attack by Sentinels leaves the mansion in ruins, so the idea that these heroes were killed off during the fight does make sense, yet it feels lazy and doesn't give these characters the respect they deserve. The Russo Brothers said they wouldn't answer anything specifically relating to their fates but did add, "The history of the X-Men is really special to us. All of those characters are loved, and we thought a lot about their history. So, they feed into this movie in a very meaningful way."

The lack of Storm, Jean Grey, and others is part of a much larger problem facing the MCU today. Characters tend to make their debut and then kind of just disappear. This wasn't a problem through the first three phases, as almost every notable hero or villain who showed up there went on to appear in later projects. Since Avengers: Endgame , it has been much messier, with characters like the entire roster from Eternals not showing up again. It's especially troubling with seemingly important female characters. Captain Marvel looked destined to become one of the leaders of the Avengers, but after one box office bomb, she's suddenly nowhere to be found.

A common complaint tossed at Avengers: Doomsday so far is the lack of female characters. They found room to include someone like Gambit, who was mostly a fun small role in Deadpool & Wolverine , yet they have nothing for Captain Marvel, She-Hulk, Ms. Marvel, or even Monica Rambeau, who was literally last seen interacting with Kelsey Grammer's Beast, or at least a variant of him. America Chavez is another huge omission , as she can literally travel the multiverse on her own and somehow plays no part in the Multiverse Saga.

The fact that Avengers: Doomsday manages to make space for Nightcrawler, Beast, Gambit, Falcon, and even to bring back Steve Rogers, but can't do the same for the women of the MCU, isn't a good thing. While it's clear that the ladies of the film, like Yelena, Sue Storm, and Shuri, are going to play major roles, the cast features way more men than women. No Storm, Rogue, or Jean Grey, among others, is another example of that and we need a legitimate explanation for why. Otherwise, it's going to make Avengers: Doomsday significantly worse.

Why do you think these characters were left out of Avengers: Doomsday ? Give us your theories in the comments!

This year's Torino Film Festival opened with a valentine to British artists, as directors Stephen Frears and Mike Newell collected lifetime achievement awards ahead of a screening of "November 1963," the latest from Palme d'Or winner Roland Joffé .

Of the same generation, the three filmmakers followed remarkably similar paths. All cut their teeth on the BBC's landmark 1970s anthology series "Play for Today" before breaking into the big league with a string of 1980s and '90s classics, including "The Mission," "The Killing Fields," "Dangerous Liaisons," "The Grifters," "Four Weddings and a Funeral" and "Donnie Brasco." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories Taylor Swift's 'Law & Order: SVU' Crime Scene Evidence Board from the Emmys Goes on Display at the Paley Center (EXCLUSIVE) TV Academy Cancels Televerse for 2027 Emmy Season; Festival Will Return in Early 2028

So when Newell took the stage to accept his Stella della Mole trophy, he began by paying tribute to a friendship that took root at the University of Cambridge in the early 1960s.

"It's lovely to be in the same hall as my old friend Stephen Frears, whom I have known since I was 18 years old," he said to booming applause. "We go a ways back."

Accepting his award from Italian actress Giovanna Mezzogiorno, Newell also recalled the less-than-ideal conditions surrounding their 2007 collaboration, "Love in the Time of Cholera," which was shot in Colombia, with Javier Bardem, Liev Schreiber and Benjamin Bratt also in the cast.

"She and I made a movie in impossible circumstances, in an impossible country, of an impossible script," he quipped. "And we managed to live through it!" It wasn't always easy, he added, particularly when the crew found themselves in a helicopter unable to land because of ground fire. "They were shooting at us, and [the pilot] just didn't want to go," Newell recalled. "There was Giovanna Mezzogiorno, on my arm, being shot at, being like, 'F— all this!'" blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Frears, meanwhile, drew plenty of laughs by thumbing post-Brexit wounds. "I'm English," he reminded the Turin crowd. "Do you remember England? Once we were European!"

Now readying on his 25th theatrical feature, the director was equally self-effacing about his prolific career. "[Directing is] all I can do," he deadpanned. "I can't do anything else. I'm helpless." Still, the work has brought him plenty of pleasure. "I've always had a good time," he admitted. "I mean, look at those actors [with whom I've worked]. I've been very lucky."

Alongside a tribute to Margarethe von Trotta, the first female director to win the Golden Lion for 1981's "Marianne and Juliane," the opening ceremony also doubled as a stealth "Pulp Fiction" reunion, with John Travolta and Maria de Medeiros both receiving lifetime achievement trophies.

Accepting her award in fluent Italian, the Portuguese actress offered a few thoughts on the relationship between language and performance.

"Every language has its own point of view, but I have to say that Italian was a dream for me, and I learned it while filming ‘The Remains of Nothing’ with Antonietta De Lillo in Naples. I had a wonderful coach for Italian, and for Neapolitan there were 15, all with different opinions!"

"This prize is an absolute landmark," de Medeiros continued. "I'm truly honored to receive this star alongside so many extraordinary names in cinema, and we all also want to celebrate Italian cinema, which is a reference point for filmmakers all over the world."

articles.title: Vijay Sethupathi's 'Maharaja' Producer Confirms Hollywood Remake Approach as WAVES Film Bazaar Panel Weighs Whether Indian IP Can Travel
articles.summary: The success in China of Tamil thriller "Maharaja" has led to an approach from a Hollywood agency for remake rights, producer Sudhan Sundaram confirmed during a panel at WAVES Film Bazaar, the market held alongside the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Goa, where the film was held up as an example of […]
articles.content:
The success in China of Tamil thriller " Maharaja " has led to an approach from a Hollywood agency for remake rights, producer Sudhan Sundaram confirmed during a panel at WAVES Film Bazaar , the market held alongside the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Goa, where the film was held up as an example of the growing reach of Indian film intellectual property (IP).

Produced by Sundaram, the Chennai-based founder of Passion Studios, the 2024 Vijay Sethupathi starrer reportedly grossed approximately INR910 million ($9.6 million) at the Chinese box office. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories Agatha Christie Series 'Tommy & Tuppence' Coming to Channel 5 in the U.K.

Titled "From Local Hit to Global IP: Rooted in India, Reimagined for the World" and moderated by Rajeev Masand, the panel featured Nikhil Madhok, director and head of originals at Prime Video and Amazon MGM Studios India; Saugata Mukherjee, head of content at Yash Raj Entertainment; Ruchikaa Kapoor Sheikh, director at Netflix India; and Paolo Teta, head of business affairs at LSPG. The speakers commended the success of "Maharaja."

"The fact that we are talking about whether Indian stories are truly traveling tells you something, which is that we still haven't had that global moment where something is consistently traveling," Madhok said. "What we see with Korean content, that breakthrough moment hasn't happened for India yet. The journey has begun, and we're well on the path to doing that."

Authentic, locally rooted stories have a better chance of standing out internationally than those derived from existing formats or trends, Madhok said, citing Prime Video series "Made in Heaven" and "Raakh" as shows that had traveled beyond expectations. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

For Kapoor Sheikh, India has always been a storytelling powerhouse, and streaming has made language less of a barrier. "Revenge, love, first love, heartbreak, a mother's love for a child – these are so universal that we're hoping the audience comes back to that world to continue exploring it. What, therefore, is local and what is global? That's something to question," she said.

Mukherjee pointed out that Indian films such as "Mother India" (1957) and "Dilwale Dulhania Le Jayenge" (1995) have traveled internationally for decades. With streaming, he said, the lines between local and global have started to blur, and the distinction now is between a story finding viewers abroad and its IP being adapted or remade for other markets. "Have the IPs traveled? Have we got a show which is being remade into 50 other languages? Not yet," he said.

The discussion also turned to franchises and the risk of losing sight of the standalone film. Madhok said the first priority must be to make a compelling film and establish its characters, with an extension following only if there is another worthwhile story to tell. Mukherjee agreed that a franchise should be driven by story rather than the commercial appeal of extending a hit, suggesting that some stories draw their strength from remaining contained.

The panel also identified animation as an opportunity for Indian storytelling, given the country's wealth of folk narratives and cultural traditions.

Teta argued that understanding the legal and commercial framework early need not constrain creativity and can help filmmakers make informed decisions about the future use of their work. He also suggested that agreements should find ways to recognize and reward original writers if a property is later adapted.

"Come to the lawyer early. If you come late it might be too late and expensive for you," Teta told producers, urging them to weigh adaptation and remake rights when rights are acquired or a project is commissioned.

articles.title: Generative AI Indian Feature 'Maharaja in Denims,' Inspired by Sikh Ruler Maharaja Ranjit Singh, Sets April 2027 Release (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.summary: "Maharaja in Denims," author Khushwant Singh's novel about a young man who relives the life of 19th-century Sikh ruler Maharaja Ranjit Singh, is nearing the finish line as a feature-length generative AI film – one its makers say they effectively had to make three times. The team hopes to release the film by April 2027, […]
articles.content:
" Maharaja in Denims ," author Khushwant Singh's novel about a young man who relives the life of 19th-century Sikh ruler Maharaja Ranjit Singh , is nearing the finish line as a feature-length generative AI film – one its makers say they effectively had to make three times.

The team hopes to release the film by April 2027, in time for Baisakhi, the Punjabi harvest festival. Ahmedabad-based Twenty-Twenty One Studios has come aboard as co-producer and is weighing a theatrical run followed by non-theatrical distribution. Balpreet Kaur, a Punjab-based independent filmmaker, is directing and holds final creative control. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories Agatha Christie Series 'Tommy & Tuppence' Coming to Channel 5 in the U.K.

The book was optioned in July 2020 by producer Guneet Monga Kapoor, but that version never got made. Singh, who is also CEO of Intelliflicks Studios, the company producing the AI film, tells Variety the timing worked against it. The option landed in the middle of the COVID pandemic, cinemas were slow to recover, and a story spanning Ranjit Singh's reign as well as 20th- and 21st-century India was always going to be a costly gamble for a producer.

The AI route came from Gurdeep Pall, then corporate VP of incubations at Microsoft. During a visit to Chandigarh in 2023, Pall asked Singh why the book had never reached the screen and proposed trying it with generative AI. His work with OpenAI's models had convinced him the technology would mature within a couple of years to the point where a realistic feature was possible.

"It has unfolded exactly as predicted," Singh says.

The pair co-founded Intelliflicks that year and unveiled the project with a short clip in 2024. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Choosing realism over mythology or sci-fi made consistency the central problem. Production began in 2024 with Midjourney and Runway, shifted to Google Veo, with Nano Banana handling stills, then moved through Kling AI and Seedance 2.0 before wrapping on tools available on Higgsfield. ChatGPT and Google Imagen helped build early character references, and keeping faces, costumes and sets in line took heavy manual fixes with face-swapping software, Photoshop and Adobe Firefly.

Nano Banana proved the turning point, letting the team generate new camera angles and compositions from reference images with far fewer manual corrections. Even so, Singh says near-perfect shot-to-shot consistency only became achievable four or five months ago. The team rebuilt the stills for the entire film three times before locking a look. When Higgsfield began allowing moving shots to be generated straight from character sheets, switching over would have added time and money, so the team animated the stills it already had.

Performances went through a similar evolution. Early on, real actors guided them via Runway Act-One. A single person created most of the motion shots so that each character would speak, move and react the same way throughout. The short clips also gave the editor less room to shape scenes than conventional footage allows.

"For example, if a lampshade is placed at a particular spot in a two-minute scene, it must remain in exactly the same position across every generated shot, irrespective of the camera angle. Even the slightest inconsistency can disrupt the cinematic experience," Singh says.

That learning curve drove up the budget. Singh says new technology usually cuts costs to around a tenth, but the team redid close to an hour of the film three times as the tools improved. He puts the cost at more than $500,000, excluding marketing, which has yet to begin.

"Throughout this technological evolution, the creative process has remained entirely human-led. Screenwriting, direction, storyboarding, shot composition, performance evaluation and final creative decisions remain with our filmmaking team. AI is the technology that helps us translate that vision onto the screen," Singh says.

Set in 2008, the film follows Hari Sandhu, who has flashbacks to three earlier lives: as Ranjit Singh, as a victim of Partition violence in 1947 and as a victim of the 1984 anti-Sikh violence. Kaur chose pivotal episodes from Ranjit Singh's life and added material from outside the novel to give his story more screen heft. The team stuck closely to historical sources, Singh says, but took liberties where the tools couldn't render period costumes accurately. Keeping faces and headgear consistent was also a major hurdle when production began, and some early imagery still bears the marks. Singh vetted the screenplay for accuracy with input from historians, but leaves day-to-day filmmaking to Kaur. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-articleX-uid2' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

The AI film joins a long line of Ranjit Singh projects. Last week, Katha Studios and B4 Makers Studios unveiled a big-screen biopic of the ruler , set to shoot in 2027. Actor-politician Raj Babbar's series "Maharaja Ranjit Singh" ran on public broadcaster Doordarshan from 2010 to 2011, while Contiloe Pictures' "Sher-e-Punjab: Maharaja Ranjit Singh," with Damanpreet Singh in the title role, aired on Life OK in 2017. Feature versions have proved harder to get off the ground. Babbar's planned film "The Lord of Five Rivers: Maharaja Ranjit Singh" was shelved, and "Border" director J.P. Dutta lined up a Ranjit Singh biopic after his 2018 war film "Paltan." Ranjit Singh's son Duleep Singh, the last Sikh maharaja, was the subject of Kavi Raz's 2017 feature "The Black Prince," starring Satinder Sartaaj.

The music is entirely human-made. Every song was written, composed and performed by people, and dubbing and narration were recorded with actors in the studio. Playback singer Sukhwinder Singh sang two versions of the title track, composed by up-and-coming singer Hargun Kaur, after the team also considered Rahat Fateh Ali Khan, Wazir Patar and Daler Mehndi. Recorded in Mumbai, the track pairs modern production with traditional instruments of 19th-century Punjab. Internet sensation Inayat Kaur Bajaj makes her film debut, Punjab-based Azaad and Gurprasad Singh composed and performed several tracks, and the lyricists include Harmanjit Singh, known for "Rani Tatt," as well as Ferro Fluid, Azaad and director Kaur.

On copyright, Singh relays Pall's view that there are two separate questions. What data the AI models were trained on is one for the companies that own them. How Intelliflicks uses those models is the studio's responsibility, and it avoids drawing on any style or IP that belongs to a person or company.

Singh pushes back on concerns that AI filmmaking will put actors, animators and other crew out of work, pointing to a century of the industry adopting new tools, VFX among them.

"Having made this film we see a need for human creativity and talent, from storytelling to cinematography to music. Sometimes the specific roles change but human involvement will be needed to make compelling cinema with AI," he says.

Glitches may remain, Singh concedes, but he likens them to the flaws of the earliest motion pictures. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-articleX-uid3' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

"I definitely see 'Maharaja in Denims' as an experiment, and a successful one at that, because technically, it will be the first full-length generative AI film rooted in realism, and it will be there for everyone to see," he says.

Intelliflicks is already exploring an adaptation of Singh's next novel, "The Opium Toffee," a love story set in Punjab during the 1980s, and has a spy script and a war film in development. The company is also open to partnering with outside filmmakers on hybrid productions.

articles.title: These 4 Unadaptable Fantasy Books Actually Became 10/10 Movies, But They Could Have Gone Wrong
articles.summary: Movie adaptations are all the rage in the 21st century. While film has always adapted stories from outside media, even back in the early days of cinema, there were certain works that have been considered unadaptable, especially when it comes to fantasy novels. Books and movies are very different pieces of media and the reason […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Movie adaptations are all the rage in the 21st century. While film has always adapted stories from outside media, even back in the early days of cinema, there were certain works that have been considered unadaptable, especially when it comes to fantasy novels. Books and movies are very different pieces of media and the reason is simple – scale. While both of them are stories, one is only a few hours long, whereas the other can take days and weeks to get through. The amount of detail is up to the author, but fantasy books are one place where the creators often go into exhaustive detail about the worlds they've created and this has meant that many thought them unadaptable. However, Hollywood was able to prove them wrong.

There have been several big name fantasy series that have been adapted into brilliant movies, but here's the thing – it could have gone terribly wrong. These stories were thought to be unadaptable for good reason and the fact that these four fantasy novels got made into such great movie was always a craps shoot. In fact, one of them is a strange paradox that is both an amazing series and also a complete failure of an adaptation.

Studio Ghibli is one of the best anime studios ever , responsible for some of the greatest films, animated or otherwise, of all-time. Hiyao Miyazaki made a name for himself 1984's Nausicaä and the Valley of the Wind , and started Ghibli in 1986 with Castle in the Sky . Also in 1986, another creator was releasing a work of their own that also had the world "castle" in the title – Howl's Moving Castle by Dianna Wynn Jones. The novel starred Sophie, the eldest daughter of a family living in a world where the rules of fantasy fiction reign supreme. After being cursed by the Witch of the Wastes, she takes a job with the wizard Howl and is given a chance to reverse her curse, but only if she is able to get Howl to break his contract with the fire demon Calcifer.

Howl's Moving Castle is part of that strain of meta-fantasy stories that were coming up in the British literary scene at the time, and stories like this can be a nightmare to adapt. In a lot of ways, the story is about the tropes of fantasy novels coming to life and moving those kinds of stories to a new medium, especially one so unlike novels like film, could have ruined it. However, Miyazaki and company were able to make the movie work beautifully. There's a certain symmetry in the history of the book and Ghibli that actually feels like something from Howl's Moving Castle , making it all the more interesting.

Speaking as someone who grew up in the '80s, there are few fantasy movies more beloved by my generation than The Princess Bride . The 1987 film, directed by Rob Reiner and starring Cary Elwes, Robin Wright, Mandy Patimkin, Andre the Giant, Peter Falk, Fred Savage, Chris Sarandon, Wallace Shaw (inconceivable… that I'd leave him out), Christopher Guest, Billy Crystal, and Carol Kane is an undisputed classic. We all know the story by now – Wesley falls in love with Buttercup, she's kidnapped and forced into a marriage she doesn't want, and Wesley and his companions set out to save her. The Princess Bride is one of those movies that is basically perfect in every way or, at the very least, close enough that the differences don't matter.

The movie was based on the 1973 novel by William Goldman, who was given a chance to write the screenplay. While you can say that this is probably why the movie was so good, there was a still a lot that could go wrong. The Princess Bride is a story that thrives based on its emotional connection to the audience. Reiner was able to pick the perfect cast for the film, each of them fully inhabiting their roles. If even one of them had messed up, the movie would have fallen apart. Luckily they didn't, giving the world this indelible classic.

I want to nip this one in the bud right away, because I can already sense you getting ready to scroll down to the comment section, but Frank Herbert's Dune is not sci-fi. I know it has the trappings of sci-fi – it's set in the future and there's spaceships – but it's actually more of fantasy story. You have the Bene Gesserit witches with their weird powers, the dragon-like sandworms, a bloodline of destiny, noble family rivalries, and everyone uses blades and melee weapons. In fact, the most sci-fi thing about Dune is the politics of the story, which is basically an analogy for the petrol economy, as well as a warning to never trust charismatic leaders.

Dune was considered unfilmable when it was first released, but eventually Hollywood gave it a try. 1984's Dune is one of the most confusing '80s adaptations ever , as director David Lynch tried to figure out a way to make a story that was basically just a really long essay on why following the wrong leader is suicide for a culture and failed miserably. While I still recommend the movie to people – it's a fascinating, somewhat visceral viewing experience – it's nowhere close to being a good movie. That's why Denis Villeneuve's Dune and Dune Part 2 , and the upcoming third movie, are so impressive. We literally had proof that this movie wasn't filmable, but Villeneuve was able to shock everyone.

There was no way it wasn't going to be Lord of the Rings at number one. Lord of the Rings is the most important fantasy saga ever, helping birth the genre as we know it. J.R.R. Tolkien was a man who loved words and language and he wasn't exactly keen on having his work adapted, so while he lived the trilogy stayed on the shelves of bookstores. Christopher Tolkien was in control of his father's literary works after his death, publishing the notes and earlier versions of the various Middle-Earth stories. Christopher loved his father's work more than anyone and had an almost religious reverence for it, to the extent that he wouldn't allow adaptations for a long time. However, eventually, we'd get some pretty good animated adaptations and, in 2001, the trilogy would finally come to the big screen.

There are some out there who think it's the greatest film trilogy of all-time, but there was one rather important Middle-Earth fan who disagreed – Christopher. He felt that Peter Jackson, Phillipa Boyens, Fran Walsh, and Stephen Sinclair butchered his father's story, making it into a hollow action film that barely touched on any of his father's themes. It's an interesting situation; the person who was the greatest living authority on Middle-Earth hated the movies and considered them a failure. However, the movies are some of the most beloved of all-time, sweeping awards and building a massive franchise. While I enjoy them, Christopher Tolkien is right – the movies aren't good adaptations. They are Peter Jackson's Lord of the Rings . Lord of the Rings is a paradox, because it is both a 10/10 movie series and yet also completely unfilmable.

So, do you agree with me and Christopher Tolkien or do you think that the first person to ever experience Middle-Earth was wrong? Any movies you would have included instead of my choices? Sound off in the comment section below.

The platform, Cinedubs , has brought its audio description and closed-caption technology to the festival, so that visually impaired and hearing-impaired audiences can watch films in theaters alongside everyone else. Nitesh Tiwari's epic "Ramayana," starring Ranbir Kapoor as Rama, Sai Pallavi as Sita and Yash as Ravana, opened worldwide on Nov. 5. Filmmakers from Kyrgyzstan, Romania and Mexico said they want to be recognized for artistic merit rather than token representation, speaking on a panel about women in world cinema at the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Goa.

Titled "Her Lens, Her Legacy, Her Liberty: Women Shaping World Cinema" and moderated by Indian filmmaker Abhishek Jain, the session brought together Kyrgyz writer-director Narghiza Dotieva, Romanian Roma actress, playwright and filmmaker Alina Șerban and Mexican American writer-director Suzanne Andrews Correa. All three urged emerging filmmakers to stay rooted in their cultural and emotional experiences, arguing that authentic local stories can travel. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories Agatha Christie Series 'Tommy & Tuppence' Coming to Channel 5 in the U.K.

Dotieva, whose feature debut "Skylark" explores borderland histories, traced her interest in storytelling to her grandfather's recitations of "Manas," the Kyrgyz epic poem. She came to independent filmmaking from advertising and draws on her country's cultural heritage. She also spoke about the importance of audiences and festivals supporting stories from underrepresented regions.

Andrews Correa spoke about the decade-long journey of making her debut feature "La Cazadora" ("The Huntress"), which premiered in the World Cinema Dramatic Competition at the Sundance Film Festival in January. Set in Ciudad Juárez and starring Adriana Paz ("Emilia Pérez"), the film draws on real-life cases of feminicide and on the story of "Diana, the Huntress of Bus Drivers," the vigilante behind the killings of bus drivers in the city in 2013. Șerban, whose directorial feature debut "I Matter" explores Roma identity, faced discrimination growing up in Bucharest. She has used theater and cinema to challenge stereotypes and reclaim Roma narratives, and recalled funding rejections because her scripts did not fit conventional portrayals of the community.

Șerban also described her presence at IFFI as an emotional return to an ancestral homeland, pointing to the historical links between the Roma community and Rajasthan in northwest India.

Cole Sprouse is getting candid about the realities of being a TV actor.

During an appearance on his brother Dylan Sprouse's "Wildmen" podcast — which marked the "Suite Life of Zack & Cody" stars' first on-screen reunion in a decade — Cole reflected on his time starring on the teen drama series from 2017 to 2023 and how television has changed.

"' Riverdale ' was kind of a dying species at the time because it was as we were transitioning into the streaming model, so we would film 22 hour-long episodes a year," Cole said (via Entertainment Weekly ). blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories 'Lord of the Rings: The Rings of Power' Renewed for Season 4 at Amazon Prime Video Benjamín Naishtat’s ‘The Seven Madmen,’ With ‘I’m Still Here’ Star Selton Mello, Wraps Production

He explained that a typical TV contract is fixed for the first three years, and then allows for renegotiations. "So you are making what you initially agreed upon, and if the show is a success and they want to pick it up for a fourth season, you get the option to renegotiate after the third season," he continued. "So that’s when you start making money. Substantial money. If the show is a big success, that’s when you start actually being able to roll in it."

Cole, who has mainly worked in film since "Riverdale," added that TV is just not as lucrative as it once was.

“If a show is a success, regardless, across the board, it is a great launching pad and vehicle for the future of anyone’s career,” he said. “However, the days of cutting your teeth in relative anonymity and making your bag and getting your 10,000 hours on a long-running, consistent, stable work in television is gone. Elsewhere in the episode, Cole and Dylan also discussed the effect being child stars had on them. In addition to "Suite Life," the twins starred together in "Friends," "Big Daddy" and the spinoff "Suite Life on Deck."

"What happens a lot with us, which I find very interesting, is that when people come up as fans — which is always flattering — they'll make sure to let you know which one of you is their favorite," Dylan said.

articles.title: Mark Cousins Backs Kyrgyzstan-Set Refugee Drama 'A Requiem in Bishkek,' a FIDMarseille Prize Winner (EXCLUSIVE)
articles.summary: Mark Cousins, the Northern Irish filmmaker behind "The Story of Film: An Odyssey," is executive producer on "A Requiem in Bishkek," the first feature from Indian director Di Sica Ray, which took the Claudia Cardinale Foundation Award at FIDMarseille. The India-France co-production world premiered in the French festival's First Film Competition. The prize rewards emerging […]
articles.content:
Mark Cousins , the Northern Irish filmmaker behind "The Story of Film: An Odyssey," is executive producer on "A Requiem in Bishkek," the first feature from Indian director Di Sica Ray, which took the Claudia Cardinale Foundation Award at FIDMarseille.

The India-France co-production world premiered in the French festival's First Film Competition. The prize rewards emerging filmmakers and backs debut features that push boundaries. Related Stories Curry Barker’s ‘Anything But Ghosts’ to Release in Premium HDR by Barco - Film News in Brief 'You Can See Everything' Gets Digital Release

Played in English and Russian, the film centers on a South Asian refugee in Kyrgyzstan who makes experimental work from discarded 16mm film stock. He lives alone in a mountain garage belonging to a Pakistani businessman and picks up spare cash looking after a cricket farm run by a Chinese man. His efforts to interest a local producer in his screenplay stall because of his refugee status. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Walks through a cityscape of Soviet-style buildings bring racist abuse that reopens old wounds. His one sanctuary is the city museum, where he finds calm among the paintings of Isaac Levitan.

When rioting erupts, he loses his job and everyone he leaned on. Shattered, he throws himself into cameraless animation, and the abstract images he projects onto his wall draw him into a mystical realm that becomes his last refuge.

Cousins tells Variety that a cut was sent to him and he agreed to lend his name as executive producer, a role he described in this case as being its advocate on the festival circuit.

"I loved its tenderness, solitude and somnambulance, and how these relate to its politics of migration," Cousins said. "I was lucky enough to know Mani Kaul, and I think he would have loved 'A Requiem in Bishkek.' As would Sergei Paradjanov I think. It is part of a very rich seam in cinema." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Kaul was the Indian modernist behind "Uski Roti," while Paradjanov directed the Soviet-era classic "The Color of Pomegranates."

Marilyn Brakhage, widow of American avant-garde filmmaker Stan Brakhage, called the film moving, sorrowful and tragic, and said that at a time of crises and conflict around the world, finding greater empathy for people adrift in a hostile world matters deeply.

"At the same time, it is so profoundly beautiful in its evocation of the restorative powers of Art, and of the world of Art as being that place, the only place, 'that truly welcomes my soul' as the character says," she said. "… But as Stan would have said, 'It's not just about our relationship to the Earth, but our connection to the stars.' He would have been deeply honored by your remembrance of him."

Ray has spent the past decade moving between Russia, Kyrgyzstan and other ex-Soviet states, working as a freelance photojournalist. He has previously made shorts in Kyrgyz, English, Japanese and Italian, and he edited "A Requiem in Bishkek" himself.

"I believe my art can help relieve humanity of its obsession with hatred towards fellow human beings," Ray said in his director's statement.

Thanikachalam S.A. produced the film, with Carine Peyrieres as associate producer. Mirlan shot it, and Peter Theremin composed the music, with Ray's treatment describing a score that draws on Tchaikovsky. Rana Eid handled sound design, Lama Sawaya was re-recording mixer and Moaz Elgabry graded the picture.

The director participated in the WAVES Film Bazaar , the market component of the International Film Festival of India in Goa.

Ray's next projects will tackle political, anthropological and ethnographic subjects, often folding in magical realism and folklore drawn from Asian storytelling traditions, in keeping with the Film for People movement he follows.

articles.title: Netflix’s Twilight Reboot Can Finally Give Fans Something the Books Never Did
articles.summary: Whether you loved it or hated it, it’s undeniable that Twilight was a very successful franchise. The four-book series that was adapted into five films made bank. The films collectively grossed over 3.3 billion at the global box office, with The Twilight Saga: Breaking Dawn Part 2 making $830 million dollars alone. Throughout the late […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Whether you loved it or hated it, it’s undeniable that Twilight was a very successful franchise. The four-book series that was adapted into five films made bank. The films collectively grossed over 3.3 billion at the global box office, with The Twilight Saga: Breaking Dawn Part 2 making $830 million dollars alone. Throughout the late 2000s into the 2010s, people couldn’t stop talking about it, even just to use it as a comparative metric — note the plethora of “still a better love story than Twilight” memes.

In 2015, author Stephenie Meyer published Life and Death . Life and Death is a gender-bent Twilight , changing Bella to Beaufort and Edward to Edythe. Then, in 2020, Meyer published Midnight Sun , giving readers the tale they love, but from the perspective of the vampiric heartthrob Edward Cullen. Four years later, it was announced that Midnight Sun was getting turned into an adult animation series for Netflix. The two leads have already been cast, with casting for other roles underway, and Netflix has already greenlit the series for two seasons, as announced mere weeks ago.

With two seasons already ordered, Netflix is likely trying to dodge a familiar complaint around most of their current shows — the lengthy pause waiting for renewal and the wait caused by waiting for production to finish. Either way, this shows a lot of faith in Twilight , presuming a still-built-in audience. While there were four books to adapt for the film Twilight Saga , there is only one published book for Midnight Sun . Perhaps this two-season order is going to give the fans something the books never did.

In comparing Midnight Sun to the original Twilight novel, die-hard fans couldn’t help but notice discrepancies. While the Twilight film emphasized the scene between Bella and Edward in the meadow, the original novel glossed over it. The Twilight novel had Bella skip past it in active time, choosing instead to look back on it in narration. Meyer’s original draft contained a longer scene, including Bella’s reaction to Edward’s skin in the sunlight, but it was cut for space.

Midnight Sun , however, shows Bella’s reaction, giving fans the moment she first sees Edward Cullen in the sun. Edward notices her freak-out and her worry that he’ll catch fire, which is what happens to vampires when exposed to the sun in Twilight lore. As part of the foreword to Life & Death , the genderbent Twilight , Stephenie Meyer expressed her rationale towards missing scenes. For her, around 10% of her additions were things she wished she’d done the first time around, but that hadn’t occurred to her. These could be items anywhere from an idea she wished she’d explored earlier, or conversations that were left out but should’ve been included.

With that in mind, it’s likely that the animated series might give fans of the book scenes and insights not present in the literature. Those associated with the production of the Midnight Sun animated series have discussed working with Meyer, emphasizing her enthusiasm for the show and for television in general. It’s unclear whether Meyer is expected to put out book sequels to Midnight Sun , but her suggesting ideas to the writers’ room doesn’t seem out of the question.

Midnight Sun is a long book. It’s longer than Twilight by a considerable amount, totaling 658 pages in all, so it wouldn’t be out of the question to divide the book evenly in two between the two seasons. It’d also make sense to speed up the pacing. When Midnight Sun came out, it was criticized for its adherence to the original series and the “glacial pace” it moved at. As a rewrite of Twilight , it makes sense that it wants to stay as close to the successful Twilight as possible, but there’s a difference between what can work for a novel and what can work for a television show. Adaptations inevitably always change something.

What Midnight Sun should do is keep the essentials for season one, giving viewers insights into Edward Cullen’s relationship with his sister and the important scenes with Bella. But by sticking to the essentials — and whatever new additions the writers can cook up — the series has a chance to go beyond Midnight Sun as a novel. Midnight Sun, the series, has the chance to give new insights into Eclipse, New Moon, and Breaking Dawn .

While the show is pitched as primarily going into Edward’s internal struggles, it also has a chance to further develop the Quileute characters, giving them more depth and letting them feel less like stereotypes. A common critique of the original book series, the movies, and even Midnight Sun is how they often felt like B-characters, even as Jacob Black is supposed to be Edward’s love rival for Bella. It’d be a smart movie for Netflix to make on their part, and it would give them more characters to explore. While the novels are written in a strict first-person limited, it’s to be seen whether the TV show will take the same approach.
