articles.title: 5 Fictional Worlds That Look Epic on Screen But Would Be Total Nightmares to Live In
articles.summary: There's something cathartic about escaping into a made-up world, isn’t there? For most people, daily life is mundane. Additionally, the real world can seem to be a bit boring or uninteresting. And if you enjoy watching movies, then real life can feel really underwhelming—real quickly. But before you go wishing you could escape into your […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google There's something cathartic about escaping into a made-up world, isn’t there? For most people, daily life is mundane. Additionally, the real world can seem to be a bit boring or uninteresting. And if you enjoy watching movies, then real life can feel really underwhelming—real quickly. But before you go wishing you could escape into your favorite fictional world, you should take the time to seriously consider what you’d be wishing for. It might come back and bite you.

On paper—and especially on the screen—many of these worlds look breathtaking. But upon looking a little more closely at their day-to-day lives, you'll find that they are not as inviting as they seem. We're talking about murderous beasts, authoritarian regimes, strange standards of behavior, and dangerous scenarios that make it feel like surviving just one Monday morning would be an achievement. So, here are five fictional worlds that look amazing on camera but would be deadly to live in—and honestly, I think I'd prefer to stay right here!

Westeros is one of those fictional worlds that every medieval fan dreams of living in. At first, you’d probably imagine living in one of those gigantic medieval castles, going to tournaments, and having dragons fly over your head. And that would sound awesome. Well, it does until you realize there's one pretty major problem with Westeros: unless you're a super-rich noble with access to a castle, it's pretty terrible there. Speaking of which—if you are a rich and powerful leader, your life would be under enormous pressure and threat.

Firstly, the place is pretty much one giant warzone. Ordinary people tend to get caught in the crossfire between warring families, power-hungry rulers, and armies that clearly don't have an issue wiping entire villages off the map. And I haven't even mentioned the weather situation. Winters seem to go on for years, which must make for some pretty intense famine. Not to mention the White Walkers that lurk nearby. Oh, and let’s not forget that there's no modern medicine and no proper sewage system. It seems more like a situation where ignorance is bliss until you get stabbed with a sword.

Here's a world that would be totally amazing to visit or just see. Pandora is the fictional moon from James Cameron's Avatar movie. It’s also one of the most stunning science-fantasy worlds ever to be created on the big screen. There are glowing forests, giant floating mountains, and all manner of unique creatures. And the humanoid Na'vi race is in tune with the planet in such a beautiful, spiritual way that you want to be there with them.

But there is one major problem: we can't breathe the air there without some pretty serious breathing gear. Which kind of makes a walk in the woods not so relaxing! And you'll need this gear unless you'd like to face down the variety of vicious animals you'll meet there, like the Viperwolves or the Thanator. Also, there is the human corporation, the RDA, whose greed endangers the entire Pandora ecosystem… which will leave you caught in the middle of either the mining or the bombings. Gotta love Pandora… from the safe confines of a movie theater!

When we first see the Capitol in The Hunger Games , it seems pretty glamorous . There are ridiculous trends and over-the-top parties. If you have the money to be there (or if you're one of the privileged members of society), it probably seems like the best place to be. The thing is: the Capitol's not the whole country. And even if you belonged to the ruling class, you’d be surrounded by corruption, deceit, and an eventual uprising.

Elsewhere, beyond the exclusive world of the rich, are districts where hardship and hunger are part of everyday life. And then there's the Hunger Games, where children are forced into a televised fight to the death for public amusement. Imagine having to send your kids onto a game show where they're forced to fight to the death for entertainment. Again, if that’s your thing, I guess it wouldn’t be too bad if you’re willing to risk your life in that kind of competition. The government also has absolute control over information, movement, and just about everything else you can think of. There's no doubt that the Capitol has something going on in terms of high tech and some truly bizarre fashion trends, but I think I'll skip this place, too.

If you love the look of futuristic cities, then Blade Runner 's version of the future might come off as your absolute dream. Towering neon signs, huge holographic billboards, and flying cars populate the landscape. Los Angeles has never looked more spectacular, and the cyberpunk aesthetic is pretty much the most iconic you'll find in sci-fi movies. Heck, we’re almost at that point in many modern cities around the world. But if things really got sci-fi, there would be plenty of problems beyond what people already face in the real world.

First of all, its environment is pretty terrible; the skies are murky, the weather is miserable, and the population has been crowded into a dense city. And that's not even mentioning the technology. All those flying cars and advertising towers are pretty flashy, but a lot of the city is actually quite shabby and run-down. There's also the terrible danger of becoming embroiled in the world of the Replicants. These human-like androids are treated as second-class beings and hunted down by specialized law enforcement officers. And what if you found yourself as one of them? I guess that could be good or bad depending on your perspective. And we can’t forget that corporations seem to have an outsized amount of power and influence. That means you’ll either have to work as one of their puppets or be a victim of their schemes.

I think it’s safe to assume that a large portion of people would want to be a witch or wizard. Especially if it was the Wizarding World . You could use a magic wand, go shopping in Diagon Alley, and throw back a butterbeer in Hogsmeade. You could even see the floating candles in the Great Hall at Hogwarts. You might even run into Harry Potter. It's the sort of place that makes you want to open your Hogwarts acceptance letter tomorrow. But if you look beyond the magic, there's a fair amount to be concerned about.

For starters, the Wizarding World has a quite serious dark magic problem. It’s seen more than its fair share of villains. And each one has caused a significant amount of death, persecution, and attempts at wizarding domination. Dementors, the soul-sucking monsters that leave victims completely traumatized, don't exactly fill one with hope for the future either. And those guys at the Ministry of Magic have a long history of corruption, bad decision-making, and questionable leadership. Oh, and let's not forget Hogwarts, where a student might be burned in a fire, have their soul sucked out by a Dementor, be cursed by their teacher, or be hit by a Bludger flying at high speeds… But if you don't mind putting yourself in considerably more danger, you might still enjoy your stay here.

articles.content:
Before shooting began on " Possible Love ," Korean director Lee Chang-dong asked actor Sul Kyung-gu what he thought of Ho-seok, the laid-off worker he plays. Sul says the first thing he told Lee was that the character feels like him.

Lee, Sul recalls, answered, "Yes, you are like him."

The film is a Venice competition title – where it won the Silver Lion, Grand Jury prize – that also screened at the Busan and Toronto festivals. It is South Korea’s submission for the Oscars’ international feature category. Ho-seok's wife, Mi-ok (Jeon Do-yeon), works at a mask factory. Sul previously starred in Lee's "Peppermint Candy" and "Oasis." Produced by Pinehouse Film, Anonymous Content, Nowfilm and Netflix , it opened in theaters Oct. 23 and has been streaming on the platform since Nov. 6. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories ‘Golden Girls’ and 'Gilmore Girls' Writers' 'Silver Foxes' Screenplay Acquired by Alder Street Productions (EXCLUSIVE) ‘Morning Show’ Star Mark Duplass and Katie Aselton Show Off Their Three Rescue Dogs in PETA Ad (EXCLUSIVE)

Sul describes Ho-seok as "the universal or the common Korean man, where you do see sort of the macho character in him, but when you deep dive deeper, there's a lot of hurt and pain."

Being laid off, he says, is "not just about him losing his job. It is about the loss of a space that was related to his identity, losing his position within society." Ho-seok carries rage and helplessness, and "even though he's a victim, he holds a great sense of shame and guilt as well as feeling inferior," Sul says. "His pride has been trampled on."

The tools Sul had to show all that were "silences and also glances." Outwardly, he says, it had to be expressed "in a very nonchalant manner." Conveying all of that through silence, he says, was "probably the biggest challenge of mine." The camera helped by portraying him "in a very aloof or distant way," and the rest, he says, is up to viewers: "I also think a lot of it has to do with the role of the audiences in terms of how you interpret this character on your own." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

On whether Korean ideas of masculinity have moved since "Peppermint Candy," Sul says "I honestly don't quite know, but it has been three decades, so I do think there has been some changes." He says "I do sense that masculinity has changed over the years. I think it has changed into a direction that society expects it to or wants it to change." He points to "some kind of public education or control or definitely regulations that affected these things," and says "you get to see those different ways of masculinity being conveyed through media." Still, "it's all different for every individual, so it's hard for me to say."

Of his earlier shoots with Lee, Sul says "the mood overall was very heavy. You know, there was nobody that was joking around on that set." On "Possible Love," he says, "sometimes because of that light mood, I would ask myself, is it okay for the ambiance to be this light?"

"Aside from myself, the other three cast members, they really put in a lot of effort to lift the overall mood," Sul says, reading it now as the actors "trying to overcome their inner tension and fear of the characters."

Of Lee's directing, Sul says "Director Lee doesn't do much overtly. He just exists as himself." Lee "constantly challenges us to think even more about the characters," he says, calling it a "silent challenge," and "with just a single glance, he could really make us get right into that mode." Sul says "there was a part of me that wanted to go back 27 to 28 years ago, and I naturally found myself in those shoes again."

"I think just the name Lee Chang-dong means complete trust for me," Sul says. Whenever he is asked for his most representative work, "I have always said it's 'Peppermint Candy,' and I think that answer will not change in the future." He says he can say so because of the trust he has in Lee, and that on getting back together with the director after 23 years, he was "once again reminded how I was right." The trust, he says, "comes from not only knowing him through his films, but also from knowing him as a human being."

Sul says what he looks for in roles has not changed much. "It's really about a good story, also a genre maybe that I haven't done before," he says. "I just want to play characters that fit my age as well as I go on." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-articleX-uid2' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

If he may be a little more ambitious, Sul says, he would love to work with directors like Lee going forward. "I think that's really something that's true for all actors."

articles.title: Every MCU Hero That Has Already Encountered an Incursion, And If They’re Confirmed for Doomsday

articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google Incursion events are a relatively new concept to the MCU's Multiverse Saga, and while they've only barely been touched on so far, Avengers: Doomsday promises to finally put them in the spotlight. The Doomsday trailers have shown that several incursion events are on the way, with the heroes most likely working together to stop them.

Incursion events are collisions between two realities that wipe out one or both worlds, making them one of the deadliest phenomena to occur in the MCU. While tons of universes have been destroyed in the MCU, very few have been part of incursion events. An Avengers: Endgame Encore scene does feature several Loki characters witnessing an incursion, but since this scene will likely be part of Doomsday , we won't count it. So, here is every other character who has witnessed an incursion so far.

3) Doctor Strange (& His Variants) Doctor Strange is arguably the MCU hero with the most experience dabbling in the multiverse, with him being at the center of Spider-Man: No Way Home and Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness , the franchise's two biggest multiverse movies so far. Surprisingly, we have seen three different iterations of Doctor Strange witness three different incursion events, and they all occurred in the same film.

The first of these is Doctor Strange 838, the former Illuminati member who helped destroy his universe's Thanos. This version of Strange used dreamwalking in order to discover how to beat the Mad Titan. However, this inadvertently caused an incursion event. Although we don't know the exact details of which universes were destroyed, we do know that he was executed by Black Bolt for his actions.

Later in Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness , Strange 199999 meets another variant, nicknamed Sinister Strange. This Strange was corrupted by the Darkhold, and his universe was destroyed by an incursion event due to his own actions. Again, we aren't given very many details about the incursion, but we do know that Strange was there to see it all.

Finally, the end of the film sees Strange 199999 being recruited by another powerful sorcerer, who warns him that he has caused an incursion event of his own. So, the film concludes with Strange hopping into the Dark Dimension, where he heads off to try to fix it.

Benedict Cumberbatch isn't yet confirmed to appear in Avengers: Doomsday , which is shocking. However, it seems incredibly likely that he'll either have a surprise appearance in Doomsday or he'll be a main character in Avengers: Secret Wars . Strange's history with incursions means that he would definitely want to get involved in the conflict, even if he takes Doom's side for whatever reason.

The powerful sorcerer who recruits Strange at the end of Doctor Strange in the Multiverse of Madness is Clea, played by Charlize Theron. The niece of Dormammu, Clea comes to Earth in order to get Strange's assistance in stopping an incursion event that his actions have caused. The incursion seems to already be in motion by the time she appears, meaning that she has witnessed the dangers of the event.

Like Strange, Theron's Clea also isn't yet confirmed to appear in Avengers: Doomsday , which is incredibly odd. If Strange does pop up in the film, it would be a weird choice to exclude Clea, as that would ignore the big cliffhanger from the previous Doctor Strange film. It could be that Clea's recruitment of Strange is what gets both sorcerers involved in the fight against Doom, paying off the post-credits scene. However, with all of the changes that the Multiverse Saga has gone through since the 2022 film's release, there is a scary possibility that Clea may never be seen again.

Until Marvel Studios parted ways with Jonathan Majors, Kang the Conqueror was the main villain of the Multiverse Saga. While a variant named He Who Remains appears in the Loki Disney+ series, Kang properly appears as the main villain of Ant-Man and the Wasp: Quantumania , where he has become stuck in the Quantum Realm. In the film, Kang mentions that the Multiversal War between his variants has caused many incursions, meaning that both Kang and He Who Remains likely witnessed them ahead of their MCU debuts.

Majors is not confirmed to appear in Doomsday , and it is incredibly unlikely that he will. Marvel and Majors parted ways ahead of the pivot from The Kang Dynasty to Doomsday . So, it would be shocking for any Kang variants to appear, unless they are played by another actor. Doomsday could offhandedly mention how the threat of Kang was wrapped up off-screen, but of all three characters who have seen incursions, Kang is the least likely to appear in Doomsday .

Which MCU characters are you excited to see witness incursions? Let us know on the ComicBook Forum !

articles.content:
A spiritual drama made for approximately INR1.7 crore ($180,000) and declared a flop within its first week of release has crossed INR450 crore ($48 million), according to its director, Vishal Chaturvedi.

Chaturvedi described the unlikely success of " Hanuman Ansh " at a Knowledge Series panel at WAVES Film Bazaar , the market held alongside the 57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Goa. Related Stories ‘La Bola Negra’ to Receive International Star Award at Palm Springs International Film Festival (EXCLUSIVE) ‘Glee’ Reboot: ‘Sadness’ Over Naya Rivera and Cory Monteith’s Deaths Is ‘Going to Be a Part’ of the Show, Says Co-Creator Ian Brennan

The film, inspired by the life and teachings of Neem Karoli Baba, the Hindu guru known in the West as the teacher of Ram Dass, found its audience through word of mouth, social media and an unusual grassroots campaign. Chaturvedi and his team traveled from city to city, visiting cinemas and speaking directly to viewers. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

When he set out, Chaturvedi said, he wanted to make a film about Neem Karoli Baba, "a subject I had wanted to explore for years, and to ensure that my producers did not lose money."

Titled "The Layers Within: Psychology, Perception, and the Power of Storytelling" and moderated by journalist Mayank Shekhar, the session also featured Portuguese filmmaker Tiago Guedes, academic Archana R. Singh and Malayalam filmmakers Anand Ekarshi ("Aattam") and Christo Tomy ("Ullozhukku"). The panel looked at how a film's meaning can extend beyond what its maker intended.

For Singh, a film is a negotiation between two storytellers. "There is a storyteller who has made the film, and there are hundreds of storytellers in the audience who actually complete it," she said. "Once you make the film, it's not complete. It gets completed by the audience: the stereotypes, the prejudices, biases, fears, everything that they carry with them, they make their own film." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Audiences have changed too, Singh said. Where they were once passive, watching a film, internalizing it and talking to a few friends, "now they are what we call 'prosumers.' They consume as well as produce. So they cut reels out of whatever content they like, and that's how they popularize it on social media."

Ekarshi's National Film Award-winning "Aattam," a chamber drama about sexual harassment involving 12 men and one woman, was conceived for his theater group. He set out to examine the behavior and psychology of the people involved without imposing a moral judgment, and to handle the subject "in a non-cliché manner, without being very loud and preachy about it."

"Can I play with the mind of the audience?" Ekarshi said he asked himself. "I believe personally that a film will only be engaging if you make the audience participate." On where the layers emerge, he said: "My perceptions about morality or education or love or mortality… those perceptions bring that magic plus one. That, no machine can do."

Tomy said he left film school thinking the biggest challenge would be crafting a story and writing a script. "But as soon as you get out of film school, it kind of reverses. The challenge is to get funding, to get the film made, to get stars to work with you. The big learning was that it's not just an art form, it's basically a business," he said. He added that producers were reluctant to back "Ullozhukku," a somber, female-led drama starring Urvashi and Parvathy Thiruvothu.

Guedes rejected the idea that commerce dilutes a director's voice, since "all the decisions come or pass through you." "I don't believe that you are smart enough to know what's going to make a commercial success," he said. "I think when it happens, it happens because somehow, we, luckily, got in touch with the human side of people, and people got connected with our work. I don't believe in formulaic algorithms."

Chaturvedi argued that a filmmaker's intent, and the audience's ability to connect with it, matter more than surface elements such as production design, costumes or an actor's appearance. "AI can do that 2 + 2 = 4. It can't do that 2 + 2 = 5, 6, 7," he said, referring to the meanings that emerge when "you relate with the story's intent and emotions."

articles.title: This 2001 Sci-Fi Movie Explored the Multiverse Years Before Hollywood Became Obsessed With It
articles.summary: What if there was another you somewhere in the universe? Not a clone or a doppelgänger, but a truly different version of you with the same face. Perhaps that version struck it rich. Perhaps that version made a few unfortunate choices. Or perhaps that version grew up to be a superpowered assassin who just decided […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google What if there was another you somewhere in the universe? Not a clone or a doppelgänger, but a truly different version of you with the same face. Perhaps that version struck it rich. Perhaps that version made a few unfortunate choices. Or perhaps that version grew up to be a superpowered assassin who just decided the multiverse wasn't big enough for the two of you. Hollywood has spent the last several years doing that kind of "what if," but one early 2000s action flick explored alternate realities long before they became a blockbuster obsession.

This film didn't require a vast cinematic universe or a web of complicated superhero backstories to make the concept work. It had one martial arts legend playing multiple versions of himself, a premise that ensured every interaction was truly dangerous, and a surprisingly ambitious idea about one's sense of self and the desire to become more than you are. And of course, there were tons of amazing action sequences.

The One arrived in 2001 with a pretty unusual premise for an action movie. The sci-fi flick starred Jet Li and was directed by James Wong. The story was set in a multiverse where alternate versions of the same person existed across different worlds. An organization called the Multiverse Authority kept an eye on travel between these realities, and it was tasked with maintaining stability. Someone had to think that was a bad idea. Check the trailer and you'll see this movie was definitely ahead of its time. It might have had the most compelling plot, but overall, it's a great watch for fans of science fiction and martial arts action.

And that someone was Gabriel Yulaw. Li plays the former Multiverse Authority Agent (M.V.A.) who learns that each time one of his counterparts dies, that person's life energy is redistributed among all the surviving versions, making each of them more powerful. Instead of just settling for one enhanced version of himself, Yulaw begins to track down his counterparts across the multiverse to become the strongest he can be. He even runs into a certain MVA agent named Evan Funsch, played by Jason Statham . His ultimate goal is to eliminate the other versions of himself and become an almost godlike incarnation called The One. The one problem? Gabe Law, also played by Li, is a Los Angeles County sheriff's deputy still standing between him and that goal. That is an excellent setup for an action movie, especially one in which the hero and villain can literally stare in the mirror to see their greatest enemy.

The fun of the premise is that the movie takes one of the harder science fiction concepts and makes it easily digestible as an action hook. Every other version represents another possibility. Every encounter adds another spike in the drama. And having to go to war with someone who might as well be himself allows Li to deliver something that most action stars can't quite deliver. He gets to fight his own mirror image with exactly the same skills. It's like a martial arts film that accidentally strolled into a science lab and started smashing things.

Today, it almost seems like audiences don't even flinch when a film introduces a new universe or an alternate version of a main character. The multiverse has become a normal part of blockbuster storytelling. Marvel has built several major storylines around the concept, while animated hits like Spider-Man: Into the Spider-Verse turned alternate realities into an expansive playground. We see the concept in all kinds of sci-fi stories and even anime. But in 2001, The One took the concept in a quite different direction. It wasn't concerned with collecting countless versions of recognizable heroes. Instead, it was interested in what would happen if a person decided the other versions of himself were his rivals.

This is where Yulaw gets more interesting than the typical martial arts movie villain. He sees his alternate selves as wasted potential. By killing them, he can absorb their life energy and become stronger than any individual version of himself. Gabe offers a very different perspective. He's the type of guy who's content with his wife and his job as a police officer. He doesn't need to become all-powerful or smite a bunch of multiversal opponents to feel unique. The conflict introduces a much more philosophical notion to the proceedings, sandwiched between flying fists and acrobatic leaps. It also provides a fun way of giving Jet Li a couple of different characters to play.

articles.title: Ashutosh Gowariker Wants IFFI Goa to Be a First-Stop Festival for Filmmakers, Rules Out 'Lagaan' Sequel
articles.summary: Ashutosh Gowariker wants filmmakers around the world to pick the International Film Festival of India (IFFI) as the place to launch their films. In his first year as festival director, the "Lagaan" and "Swades" filmmaker thinks that could take five years. "Every filmmaker, big, small, whoever, their first destination is Cannes," Gowariker tells Variety in […]
articles.content:
Ashutosh Gowariker wants filmmakers around the world to pick the International Film Festival of India (IFFI) as the place to launch their films. In his first year as festival director, the "Lagaan" and "Swades" filmmaker thinks that could take five years.

"Every filmmaker, big, small, whoever, their first destination is Cannes," Gowariker tells Variety in Goa, where IFFI's 57th edition is underway. If Cannes doesn't work out, he says, filmmakers move on to Locarno, Venice and Berlin. IFFI isn't at the top of their radar, and it comes at the very end of the year. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories ‘Morning Show’ Star Mark Duplass and Katie Aselton Show Off Their Three Rescue Dogs in PETA Ad (EXCLUSIVE) Elliot Page and Chris Columbus Board Queer Dark Comedy ‘Callback’ as Executive Producers (EXCLUSIVE)

"So I feel that something needs to be done in which a filmmaker in the world should feel… this time I want to open in IFFI. We need to build that. Might take five years, but work towards that right from now," Gowariker says. He wants filmmakers to come to IFFI for what the festival can do for them, not just because it's in Goa.

Gowariker took over from "Elizabeth" director Shekhar Kapur, who had asked him to chair the international jury in the first year of his tenure. That gave Gowariker a close look at how Kapur ran the event. He was appointed two days before Cannes and reckons that cost him five months of preparation time.

He isn't trying to rank IFFI against Busan, Tokyo and Shanghai yet. "I said, listen guys, we need to compete with ourselves first. Let's get our house in order," Gowariker says. He wants this year's best effort on programming and hospitality, working within a limited budget. Standing alongside other festivals will take time and won't happen in a year.

"Like a filmmaker, you make your movie. Make it best. If it travels, it travels," he says. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Gowariker has run the festival the way he would make a film. He treats IFFI's departments like the heads of department on a shoot and keeps them working to a shared visual and thematic design. His films have taglines – "Lagaan" was "Once Upon a Time in India" and "Swades" was "We, the People" – so he gave IFFI a theme too: "Stories Without Borders."

He says IFFI has been missing several sections, among them animation and documentary, and he has brought them in. The government's Mumbai International Film Festival (MIFF) covers those forms, but it only runs every two years. This year IFFI is holding a red-carpet gala for the MIFF winners and has added a strand of films about films, which Gowariker describes as an underrated genre.

"Because a number of animation and feature documentary filmmakers that are making films, they're not getting an outlet for it," he says.

Short films have made a soft start this year, and Gowariker also wants to include student films.

His team also set a policy of making the festival inclusive of all of India's cinemas. As an example he points to the opening film of the non-feature section, "Becoming," a Ladakhi film by Leena Yadav. Ladakh has made very few films, and he hopes the slot will encourage local filmmakers there to tell their own stories.

At IFFI's WAVES Film Bazaar , Gowariker's focus has been making sure participants can meet the people they came to see. He relied on teams that have run the event for between five and 10 years and gave it small nudges rather than an overhaul.

"Soft nudges, because after all, it is a government-run festival. You have to be careful about how you navigate all that," Gowariker says.

One thing he would like to fix is the distance between the screening venues and the Bazaar, which makes it hard to move between films and meetings. He suggests building hangar-style spaces at the Kala Academy venue. He also wants to bring the Creative Minds of Tomorrow hangar closer to the main action next year, saying it is currently too remote.

Gowariker has no contract for the role, which he describes as honorary. Kapur served a two-year term. Gowariker can't remember a filmmaker leading the festival before Kapur. Civil servants have usually held the post.

This year is also the 25th anniversary of "Lagaan," which has been celebrated with screenings in London, Melbourne and Singapore before reaching Goa. Gowariker says he and star Aamir Khan got so many requests that they let anyone who wanted to celebrate go ahead, whether or not the two of them could be there. IFFI is likely to be the last stop. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-articleX-uid2' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Gowariker first saw "Pyaasa" as a teenager. He has told his own children to watch it, along with "Mother India" and "Mughal-e-Azam," which also came out before his generation.

"Little did I know that I'll have a film of mine which is getting introduced to generations like that," he says.

He now meets nine- and 10-year-olds whose parents have shown them "Lagaan."

"I find that overwhelming. I find that amazing," Gowariker says.

A sequel has crossed his mind more than once. He has played with ideas like Bhuvan, the lead character played by Khan, traveling to England at the Queen's invitation and the return of antagonist Captain Russell.

"Then I realized that no, it cannot be touched. Just leave it as is. Anyway, I don't believe in sequels," Gowariker says.

His next film, "Lalkaara," starring Khan, is cricket-themed. Beyond that, he says nothing can be revealed yet, because the team is planning a campaign ahead of the shoot. Production begins in 2027, and he will have to fit festival work around it. He doesn't expect to travel to festivals in the first four months but plans to do so during post-production.

"I'll have to remove time from my shoot to just sit with the teams and keep the planning going," Gowariker says.

He hasn't settled the details yet. "I really want to make a bigger impact to IFFI next year," he says.

When this edition ends, his team will review what worked and what didn't. After two weeks off in December, they will start building relationships with other festivals in January, beginning with Sundance.

articles.title: UK Prime Minister Promises To Get Tough On NDAs After "Watershed" Russell Brand Sentencing
articles.summary: The UK Prime Minister has promised to tackle non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) following the Russell Brand rape sentencing. articles.content:
The UK Prime Minister has promised to tackle non-disclosure agreements ( NDAs ) following the Russell Brand rape sentencing.

Andy Burnham intervened in the debate by calling Brand a "watershed moment, not just for the culture of the entertainment industry but for us as a nation."

Brand's 10-year sentence for rape and the allegations against David Walliams , which Walliams denies, have re-energized the debate around NDAs being used to silence women in entertainment.

New laws stating NDAs can no longer gag employees who have suffered harassment or discrimination have been brought forward to January and Burnham, who was making some of his first public comments about Brand, said he wants to go further by extending to "freelance employees and fans who experience abuse," two groups of people that relate to the Brand case. Phillipa Childs, the head of broadcasting union Bectu, said Burnham's government must "urgently reassure workers in the creative industries that freelancers and other self-employed workers will have the same protections as employees, or risk creating a giant loophole in this ban." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article1-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid","mid-articleX","mid-article","300x251"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[2,2],[300,250],[620,350],[300,251],[501,282],[3,3],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366]]) .exemptFromSleep() .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Watch on Deadline if ( !window.pmc.harmony?.isEventAdScheduledTime() ) { pmcCnx.cmd.push(function() { pmcCnx({ settings: { plugins: { pmcAtlasMG: { iabPlcmt: 2, } } }, playerId: '32fe25c4-79aa-406a-af44-69b41e969e71', playlistId: '0199e506-e642-7728-8264-463efe71337b', }).render("connatix_contextual_player_div"); }); } else { // This should only be get called when page cache is not cleared and it's event time. window.pmc.harmony?.switchToHarmonyPlayer(); } Related Stories News Channel 4 News Boss Emails Staff About NDAs After Issue Rears Head Again In Wake Of Russell Brand & David Walliams News Susan Sarandon Joins Natalie Dormer, Richard Armitage & Susan Wokoma In Signing Open Letter Calling For Entertainment Industry To "Acknowledge Role It Plays" In Enabling Bad Behavior

Writing in The Guardian, Burnham confirmed the government is also looking at "staggering the age of consent" to prevent men like Brand and Walliams having sex with teenagers aged 16 and 17 when they are in their 20s and older.

"I will keep working to make sure NDAs can’t be used to silence others… while still keeping victims’ identities protected if that is what they want," wrote Burnham. "This is about rebalancing the scales of power away from perpetrators and towards victims."

Burnham quoted the judge in the Brand case, who said: "Whatever women wear, wherever they go, indeed whatever they drink, they retain the right to say no and to demand justice from the criminal courts."

articles.title: John Travolta Honors His Audience at Torino Lifetime Achievement Award Ceremony: 'You Allowed Me to Fly'
articles.summary: Honored with a lifetime achievement tribute at the Torino Film Festival, John Travolta chose to share the spotlight with a special someone: You. “Thank you for giving me the most beautiful career,” he said, his voice trembling with emotion as he dedicated the festival prize to his audience. “For the last 50 years, I've been […]
articles.content:
Honored with a lifetime achievement tribute at the Torino Film Festival , John Travolta chose to share the spotlight with a special someone: You.

“Thank you for giving me the most beautiful career,” he said, his voice trembling with emotion as he dedicated the festival prize to his audience. “For the last 50 years, I've been able to explore and give audiences so many different characters. You've offered me the opportunity to sing, to dance and to play characters I would never have dreamed of.” blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories Netflix Closes $380 Million Acquisition of Radford Studio Center 'Shaun the Sheep: The Beast of Mossy Bottom' Directors on 'Game of Thrones' Easter Egg and the 'Challenge' of Filming Michael Jackson's 'Thriller' Dance in Stop-Motion

“So, big thanks to you for letting me do what Shakespeare asks of us: to be, or not to be,” Travolta continued. “You allowed me to be. You never clipped my wings. You allowed me to fly so beautifully, on the screen and in the air.”

Flanked by artistic director Giulio Base and director Roland Joffé, the American star was on-hand to kick off this year’s Torino Film Festival with the international premiere of Joffé’s “ November 1963 ,” which casts Travolta as a Chicago mafioso intimately involved in the JFK assassination. The actor-turned-filmmaker will also stick around to present his directorial debut “Propeller One-Way Night Coach,” which now lands in Turin after launching in Cannes.

Stepping behind the camera came easy, Travolta explained, because "after 50 years of making films, nothing really surprised me."

"I watched directors do great work, not-so-good work, and mediocre work," he said at the opening ceremony. "So I collected everything I admired about the great directors and kept it in my mind like a library. Then, at a later age, I used all the things I felt worked and eliminated all the things that did not, and I made a little film that was perfection." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

He also gave attendees a glimpse of his personal cinematic tastes and his working methods.

"I'm a bit of a snob," he said of his own pantheon. "I like classic cinema. I like Fellini, and De Sica, and Bertolucci, and Lelouch and Truffaut. I enjoy the stories that go deeply into the soul. That's my favorite kind of film."

The tribute kicked off with a rousing career-highlights reel, with excerpts from "Pulp Fiction," "Get Shorty," "A Civil Action," "Hairspray," "Primary Colors," "The Thin Red Line," "Mad City," "Phenomenon," "Blow Out" and "Face/Off" bookended by Travolta's emblematic musical performances in "Saturday Night Fever" and "Grease."

The audience's audible enthusiasm may even have contributed to Travolta's emotion, as the crowd stomped, clapped and sang along, beginning its ovation well before he took the stage.

When he did, he began by explaining where he starts when stepping into a new role. "With every character, I decide first how they move through space," he said. "[I first figure out] how they move through the air, and then I add to that."

articles.title: Wacom and India's IICT Ink Pact at IFFI Goa With Scholarships, Manga and Anime Masterclasses
articles.summary: Eighteen students at the Indian Institute of Creative Technologies (IICT), India's national center of excellence for animation, visual effects, gaming, comics and extended reality (AVGC-XR), will have half their tuition covered under a pact with Wacom India signed at the International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Goa. Wacom India is the local arm of […]
articles.content:
Eighteen students at the Indian Institute of Creative Technologies (IICT), India's national center of excellence for animation, visual effects, gaming, comics and extended reality (AVGC-XR), will have half their tuition covered under a pact with Wacom India signed at the International Film Festival of India (IFFI) in Goa.

Wacom India is the local arm of Japan-based Wacom Co., Ltd. Animators, VFX artists and game developers around the world work on its parent company's pen displays and creative tablets, and studios using its technology include Disney, Pixar, DreamWorks, Sony, Netflix, Marvel and ILM. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories 'Thursday Murder Club' Author Says Wife's Casting in Netflix Adaptation Was a Coincidence: 'It Had Nothing to Do With Me' Lionsgate Play Casts AI Actor Yug R.Ai in Series 'Eklavya,' Partners With Google Cloud (EXCLUSIVE)

The 50% scholarships go to students in each of IICT's three two-year diploma courses – Animation Film Design, Interactive Video Game Design and Development, and Post Production and VFX. Eligible students coming from out of town can also get help with accommodation.

The memorandum of understanding goes further. It commits the partners to 10 creative contests carrying Wacom branding, to run through December 2027, plus quarterly masterclasses in which artists and industry experts from both Japan and India will teach manga, anime and other disciplines. Qualifying IICT students and faculty will be able to buy Wacom products at reduced prices.

"Japan has shaped some of the most influential traditions in animation, manga, gaming and visual storytelling, while India has a deep and diverse storytelling heritage of its own," said Ashish Kulkarni, IICT's founding director. "This partnership with Wacom creates a meaningful bridge between these two creative strengths, giving students opportunities to learn from global practitioners, experiment with professional technology and take their original ideas to a wider audience." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

IICT and Wacom will also set up a joint global showcase for student work covering game art, animation, character design, concept art and digital illustration. Separately, the deal opens the door for IICT to appear on Wacom's tablet packaging and on Pixel Perch, the company's creator platform. Both elements depend on implementation plans to be agreed by the two sides.

"A student's transition from training to employment in AVGC-XR depends increasingly on what they can demonstrate, not only what they have studied," said IICT CEO Vishwas Deoskar. "That is why this partnership goes beyond scholarships. The 10 creative contests and quarterly masterclasses will put students through industry-oriented briefs, while access to professional tools and a portfolio showcase will help convert that learning into demonstrable work."

Yano Koji, global head of Wacom's Creative Experience Unit, pointed to the company's Japanese roots and long history with artists, saying it sees major potential in closer creative ties between India and Japan. "Both countries have rich creative traditions, and there are exciting opportunities for knowledge exchange, skill development and collaboration across animation, manga, gaming and digital content," he said.

The pact extends an existing collaboration between the two organizations. Rajiv Malik, senior director at Wacom India, linked it to India's push to nurture its so-called Orange Economy and build an AVGC-XR sector that can compete globally.

"Through the IICT–Wacom Scholarship Program, our aim is to make specialized creative education more accessible and empower talented young people to pursue careers in animation, gaming, visual effects and other emerging creative disciplines," Malik said.

articles.title: This Forgotten '90s Sci-Fi Series Was a Strange Experiment, But It Held a Much Bigger Mystery
articles.summary: And so there was television that wasn't afraid to be a little strange. Before the sci-fi shows of your youth had to have a four-tiered mythology and, say, a 10-season streaming deal, they could just be a little weird sometimes. Sometimes they survived, and sometimes they did not, and then there was Earth 2. In […]
articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google And so there was television that wasn't afraid to be a little strange. Before the sci-fi shows of your youth had to have a four-tiered mythology and, say, a 10-season streaming deal, they could just be a little weird sometimes. Sometimes they survived, and sometimes they did not, and then there was Earth 2 . In 1994, NBC aired a science-fiction series set in the not-too-distant future, about humanity's attempt to find a new home after Earth became increasingly uninhabitable. Most of humanity had already relocated to orbital space stations, but those stations weren't an ideal long-term solution. There were spaceships, strange creatures, corporate conspiracies, and a thousand questions for science-fiction fans to chew on.

But Earth 2 was never your standard space sci-fi series . It was a story about colonists who set out to find a new planet that could become home to a group of children suffering from a mysterious disease. Their destination, G889, turned out to be anything but an empty world waiting to be settled. It had a history, to say the least, and mysteries even more so. NBC only aired one season, which meant that a lot of the larger story was left up in the air. But why was the adventure to G889 so incredibly unique, and why does its story still deserve some admiration?

Earth 2 's premise was pretty ambitious from the get-go. The series, which premiered on NBC on Nov. 6, 1994, took place in the year 2192, after humanity had largely abandoned an increasingly uninhabitable Earth in favor of orbital space habitats. Led by Devon Adair, a mother desperate to save her young son, Ulysses, a group of colonists traveled aboard the starship Eden Advance to the faraway planet G889. Ulysses suffered from a mysterious disease known as the Syndrome, which affected children born in humanity's orbital habitats. The expedition was supposed to establish a new settlement called New Pacifica for the 250 families who would eventually follow. It was a pretty ambitious plan, especially considering that the fate of so many children depended on it.

After a 22-year journey, the Eden Advance reaches G889, only for the spacecraft to malfunction and crash-land thousands of miles from its intended destination. The remaining group has to make a difficult trek toward New Pacifica. The end result is a group of people fighting for survival in a world they barely understand. It gave the show the chance to revisit some of the classic sci-fi tropes of colonization and survival, and humanity's relationship with the natural world. But it also presented a surprisingly well-developed story about the conflicts that come with having very different people living together in a new world. The characters weren't always working together, and their different perspectives led to plenty of tension. Instead of typical encounters, Earth 2 took an ambitious risk and explored what happens when people arrive somewhere that already has a life of its own.

By the time the colonists set foot on the planet, intelligent life had already been living there for generations. The Terrians appeared to live in close connection with the planet itself, communicating through dreams and seemingly possessing abilities the colonists could barely comprehend. Their relationship with Ulysses became especially important after they helped cure his Syndrome. However, his newfound connection to them would create complications of its own. The scavenging Grendlers and the potentially dangerous Kobas showed just how much the colonists still had to learn about the world they were trying to make their new home.

It was a rich mythology that sent Earth 2 down an interesting path. As the survivors uncovered more about G889, they found themselves with even more questions. And then there was the Council. These guys were the powerful authority that controlled much of humanity's life in the space stations. Their interest in G889 seemed to go far beyond simply providing humanity with a new home. The Council's experiments suggested that the Terrians were essential to the planet's survival, and that eliminating them could make G889 uninhabitable. Ulysses' growing connection to the Terrians made him particularly important to that mystery.

And as for all that potential, NBC pulled the plug on Earth 2 after its first and only season, which is generally counted as 21 episodes, including its two-hour premiere. The planned season finale, " All About Eve, " aired on May 21, 1995, and revealed more about the Council's surveillance technology and the mysterious illness affecting the colonists.

The colonists discovered that malfunctioning biostat implants secretly placed by the Council were responsible for the mysterious illness affecting the expedition. Although the colonists managed to resolve that crisis, Devon's health continued to deteriorate for reasons unrelated to the malfunctioning implants. With her condition worsening, Julia placed her in suspended animation, leaving her ultimate fate uncertain. The episode raised the possibility that G889 itself might eventually reject its human visitors. NBC subsequently aired " Natural Born Grendlers " and " Flower Child ," with the former actually belonging much earlier in the story's chronology. " Flower Child " became the last episode broadcast on June 4, 1995. It was quite a way to leave viewers, especially with the colonists still trying to wrap their minds around this planet and its impossible otherness. We fans can certainly understand how frustrating the cancellation was. For an entire season, Earth 2 had been opening the door to an amazing science-fiction universe, and we only got to see through the doorway.

articles.content:
Noomi Rapace is venturing into the film and TV production space by officially launching Boom Films, co-founded with her longtime manager and production partner Stella Härnström. The London and Stockholm-based company is being backed by former Pulse Films boss Thomas Benski ’s Lumina Media .

The actor, who first captured global attention with her potent portrayal of Lisbeth Salander in the Swedish film adaptations of Stieg Larsson's Millennium Trilogy — starting with “The Girl With the Dragon Tattoo" — is ramping up a slate that currently comprises six to eight female-driven genre projects. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories 'You Can See Everything' Gets Digital Release ‘One Last Order’: Beloved Drive-Thru Worker Sighle Williams Says ‘I Miss the Community’ as Viral Netflix Doc Streams

"I've done a lot of action movies, and I've always been craving to work more with women," she told Variety. "But in so many of these films, it's me fighting men. So it's the same thing with male directors in the action [movies] sphere. Where are all the women that want that direct action?"

Boom is joining Lumina Media’s growing portfolio of businesses comprising Carrousel Studios, founded by Omar Sy, Louis Leterrier and Benski; Benedict Cumberbatch’s SunnyMarch; Yann Demange’s Wayward Films; Magna Studios, which is behind Oasis doc "Don't Look Back in Anger" and headed up by fellow former Pulse execs Marisa Clifford and Davud Karbassioun; gaming and creator economy business Creators Corp; and Arcade Media.

Lumina Media will work closely with Boom Films as a strategic partner. Besides making an unspecified investment, Lumina will provide "development expertise, commercial support and access to its international network, helping the company progress its existing slate and scale the business," according to a statement. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Oskar Pimlott, who is a former head of film at Vice and Pulse Studios, has been appointed head of film at Boom Films. Pimlott is working alongside Rapace and Härnström to develop Boom's slate, which is being kept under wraps for now, with the first projects to be announced early next year. Pimlott was recently nominated as a breakthrough producer at the British Independent Film Awards for his work on Swedish director Jonatan Etzler’s black comedy “Bad Apples.”

Boom will be working directly with filmmakers and artists to develop original projects from the ground up. "Its slate spans action, thrillers, horror and supernatural stories aimed at global audiences, alongside prestige arthouse cinema developed in collaboration with world-leading filmmakers," according to the statement. The company also aims to create original stories and IP with the potential to extend beyond film and television into other formats.

"Boom Films sort of came out of this desire to connect dots; to connect people," Rapace, who has previously served as producer on several projects, most of which she starred in, told Variety.

"I've worked with all these incredible filmmakers and actors and producers and writers all over the world," she added. "But it takes so long from an idea to sending out a film to the world. And a lot of momentum gets killed because it's too many middle hands."

Added Benski: "From the Lumina perspective as an investor, what was very attractive is that Noomi and her team are a real engine. They are really builders and I've been so impressed with what they've been able to build so far, very much in stealth. The reason for the investment is to help amplify them."

Benski noted that Lumina intends to be "a bridge between Scandinavia, Europe and the U.S." and that, in terms of financing, they "might take a big swing" on some of the projects, while others will "need market validation" from outside investors as well.

Benski said the plan is for Boom Films to start rolling out projects strategically next year "during the next few markets and festivals."

As for the company's name, Rapace said that Boom "stands for the heartbeat, but also explosions," adding: "I've always loved films that sort of explode into your mind and heart, and you don't need to always love them, but you need to remember them and sort of go back to them." blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-articleX-uid2' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Describing the slate, Rapace said it will comprise very well known IP "approached from an innovative angle," underlining that it will be about "embracing this difference to create specificity," and the budgets will be "quite varied."

Rapace said she will be starring in several of the projects in the Boom Films slate. Like many other actors who venture into production, she is now mulling plans to debut as a director — in her case, with a comedy.

"I have a really dark sense of humor, and I'm really drawn to comedies. Even though everyone sees me as this very serious, hardcore [actor], like, 'Oh she's so badass!'" she said. articles.title: 'Hershey' Review: In a Sugary Sweet Biopic, Finn Wittrock Plays the Candy Man Who Turned Chocolate Into an American Empire
articles.summary: At "Hershey," you feel like you’re 10 years old again, which is both a virtue and not. The film is a paint-by-numbers storybook biopic for the chocolate-loving child in us all – or, maybe, for an audience the movie treats as if it needed its hand held.
articles.content:
Angel Studios, in its quest to deliver movies that remind us of The Way America Used To Be, has brought back the "great man" biography — not so much the old-fashioned Hollywood biopic but, rather, movies like "Young Washington" and " Hershey ," the sort of life-of-the-plaster-saint saga you used to read in the fifth grade. These are history-based tales that are proud in their simplicity, that abolish all shades of gray, that are intended to inspire but also work on the audience because they’re so comforting . It feels good, in a certain super-square regressive way, to watch a movie about the man who popularized the American chocolate bar and was a paragon of philanthropic generosity besides. At "Hershey," you feel like you’re 10 years old again, which is both a virtue and not. The film is a paint-by-numbers storybook biopic for the chocolate-loving child in us all — or, maybe, for an audience the movie treats as if it needed its hand held. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-article-uid0' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid-article1","mid-articleX","mid","mid-article"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article") .addSize([[300,250],[2,2],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[320,480],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; }); Related Stories 'The Odyssey' Oscar Campaign Kicks Off With 8 New Revelations, From Tom Holland’s Shorter Skirt to Pattinson’s Rejected Wig and a Trojan Horse Stuck in Customs 'The Odyssey' Takes Imax to Biggest Quarterly Revenue to Date

Early on, there’s a scene that gives you that kid-in-a-candy-store feeling, because it’s all about…a kid in a candy store. Milton Hershey, played as a boy by James Kelly, has moved with his stern 19th-century Mennonite family from a dairy farm in Pennsylvania Dutch country to the bustling city of Lancaster. There, he wanders into a candy shop, where he’s welcomed by the owner and chief candy maker, played with a touch of screwball carny fervor by Richard Kind. "There’s no sweeter way to make a living," he says, offering the boy a candy called a sugar-plum swirl and then taking him under his wing as an apprentice. Milton learns the art of candy, and it’s not long before the film cuts to Philadelphia in 1882, where the adult Milton now has his own candy store with a handsome green-and-white awning. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-dsk-tab-mid-article2-uid1' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["mid","mid-article2","mid-articleX"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-article2") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[2,4],[4,2],[620,366],[300,450]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

He makes hard candy and yummy taffy, but his specialty is caramel bonbons, which he crafts with a special milk recipe. It’s the milk that gives it that luscious velvet smoothness. Milton has got the goods, and he’s a charismatic candy man besides. Finn Wittock, a veteran of Ryan Murphy series (and also "La La Land" and Mike Nichols’s 2012 stage revival of "Death of a Salesman"), is a likable actor who suggests a cross between Orson Welles and Robert Wagner. He’s got a sonorous elegance and gleaming eyes, but with a user-friendly nice-guy veneer. For Milton, making candy is a mission, but he starts off as a faltering businessman; his shop goes under, and that will happen to him again, as he struggles to find an audience for his goodies. Salvation comes in the form of a British aristocrat (Mark Ashworth) who tastes one of Milton’s caramels and puts in an order for 3,000 of them to be shipped to England for a party.

"Hershey" is a movie in which the hero has obstacles (like his unscrupulous candy-business rival), but no demons or inner conflicts. He’s just like his candies: sweet on the outside and the inside. For a while, caramel is king, but it’s chocolate that’s the future. The film colors in the period when Milton is leveraged up to his eyeballs and still searching for the perfect recipe; he figures out that milk is the key here as well. But the aspect of Milton Hershey the movie is actually most interested in is that he popularized what had formerly been elite candy. The Swiss and British chocolates that inspire him are all based on secret recipes, and they’re so expensive that few can afford them. Hershey wants to make a great candy bar that will sell for five cents, so that anybody can buy one. He pays his workers top dollar and gives them shares in the company. He’s a turn-of-the-century Willy Wonka as utopian socialist dreamer.

Wittrock makes Hershey appealingly robust in his chocolate passion, and that drew me into the movie. What keeps nudging me out of it was how sketchy it is. "Hershey" was directed Mark Waters, who did lively work in the late '90s and 2000s ("Mean Girls," "The House of Yes"), but here he skitters through a script that’s so perfunctory it treats even the invention of the Hershey’s Kiss as just one more oh-and-this-happened incident. The dew-drop-shaped candy first results from a faulty machine, but we never see Milton — or anyone else — rhapsodize about it, sharing with the audience what makes it so special. (They never even mention the silver-foil wrapping.) My own theory of the Hershey’s Kiss is that it’s a magical candy because it’s made of the very same chocolate as a Hershey bar, yet that succulent shape somehow makes it taste different. blogherads.adq.push(function () { blogherads .defineSlot( 'medrec', 'gpt-variety-article-mid-articleX-uid2' ) .setTargeting( 'pos', ["btf","mid-articleX","mid"] ) .setTargeting( 'viewable', 'yes' ) .setSubAdUnitPath("ros\/mid-articleX") .addSize([[320,480],[300,250],[300,251],[620,366]]) .setClsOptimization("minsize") ; });

Milton meets and marries the feisty Kitty (Alexandra Daddario), who loves him, spars affectionately with him, and inspires him to establish a school for impoverished children. But the desire to move back to his old homestead and build an entire town in Pennsylvania Dutch country — the factory town of Hershey, which will be part workers’ paradise, part Disneyland — is his own. They’re living the dream until Kitty starts to succumb to muscle seizures, and it turns out she has a degenerative illness, progressive paraplegia. The movie refuses to characterize her condition as tragic, but it does use it to inspire what we might call faith-based tears.

"Hershey" is a movie that makes you hungry for chocolate, and that’s part of its appeal. So is the notion that a legendary American entrepreneur could ever have been this much of a selfless gentleman. Yet the movie simulates your sweet tooth without necessarily satisfying it. Chocolate, as anyone who craves it knows, is no casual delight. There’s something orgasmic about chocolate (yes, even a Hershey bar), but in "Hershey" it’s a strictly civilized pleasure.

articles.title: The Coolest Batmobile Has Been Sold, but Even Bruce Wayne Might Flinch at the Price
articles.summary: Courtesy of Warner Bros. Pictures There are some movie vehicles that need no introduction and the Batmobile is one of them. articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google There are some movie vehicles that need no introduction and the Batmobile is one of them. As one of the most iconic movie cars ever seen on screen, the idea of owning the real thing is one that would likely be just the stuff of dreams. However, someone is now the proud owner of Michael Keaton's Batman Returns Batmobile, one of three built especially for Tim Burton's 1992 sequel and based on the designs of the original 1989 Batmobile. The version auctioned by Julien's Auctions was the action hero car, a true one-off piece of movie history that has now been purchased for an astonishing $4.39 million , although even that huge amount is something of a disappointment considering it came in under the original estimates of between $5-7 million.

The Batmobile that has now sold was the first vehicle delivered to the set for the production of Batman Returns and the auction house notes that there are several pieces of evidence that prove this is the vehicle that appears on screen in the majority of the movie's driving sequences, and it was driven by Keaton in many of those scenes. As you would expect, there are many reasons why the 1989 Batmobile would probably have sold for more than a copy made for its sequel, but a $4.39 million price tag is certainly not small change and is one of the most expensive movie props ever sold at auction. The sale was part of a larger auction, which also included many other Batman items such as Keaton's cowl/chest piece, Alicia Silverstone's Batgirl costume piece from Batman and Robin, and several pieces from the more recent Batman vs Superman and Justice League movies.

When it comes to iconic movie vehicles, a 2004 poll by UCI Cinemas put Keaton's Batmobile at the top of the list of the best screen cars ever, ahead of James Bond's Aston Martin and the minis from The Italian Job. While some people still prefer other Batman cars, with Adam West's 60s version getting an honorable mention on some polls and Christian Bale's Tumbler leading the pack in others, on the whole, there is a general consensus that the 1989 version and 1992's copycat are the ultimate iterations of one of the coolest vehicles in cinema. That is why it has been recreated in toy lines, LEGO sets, artwork and many other mediums over the years, more than any other Batmobile seen across the numerous Batman projects that have been released in the last 60 years.

However, there is nothing like the real thing, which is why this auction attracted so much attention since it was originally announced last month. In 1992, there were many Batman fans who would have never imagined that one day the actual Batmobile they were watching on screen would be sold to the highest bidder. Perhaps if they had, they might have invested money wisely over the last three decades to have a shot of putting in a bid that could snatch victory at hammer-fall. It is hard to imagine that this Batmobile will appear on the auction block again anytime in the near future, but whenever it does show up somewhere down the line, there is a strong chance it could end up selling for more than it did in this event. Maybe it is time to start saving up now for when that eventually happens.

How much would you pay to own the Batmobile? Let us know in the comments.

articles.content:
Share on X (Opens in new window) X Share on Facebook (Opens in new window) Facebook Add Us On Google The passing of Patrick Stewart on Oct. 28, 2026 was a huge shock to the entertainment industry and the millions of fans who loved his prolific body of work across the different series he performed in. Unbeknownst to the majority of the world, Stewart's cause of death was revealed as a “brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s Disease and Lewy Body Dementia,” the latter of which was the same devastating affliction Robin Williams was secretly dealing with before he took his life. Whatever struggles Stewart dealt with during his final days may forever be a secret, but what we do know is that fans will have one more chance to see him in action when Professor X joins the battle against Doctor Doom in Avengers: Doomsday later this year.

According to an interview with Entertainment Weekly , Feige and the Russos are planning on having a tribute to Stewart in Doomsday , but how that looks has not been entirely decided at this time. “We’re long done filming that movie, and he did an amazing job for us,” Feige told EW. “We’re looking now at how we can put something together that honors and respects our friend.” Feige also revealed that Stewart was offered a role in the upcoming Secret Wars film, but turned it down. Whether this was health-related or he passed for other reasons will likely never be known.

Regardless of his reasons, Doomsday will be Stewart's final appearance as the headmaster of the Xavier Institute as previously reported on this site . As the incursions on the Multiverse by Doctor Doom wreak havoc on many worlds, many believe this entry in the franchise will be a bittersweet one for the mutant side of the MCU, and may very well be the end of this on-screen iteration of Professor X. The future of the character is uncertain, but one sad note that is true is that Doomsday was the final role Stewart would perform.

Feige recalled that last day on set, and how heavy it felt after it happened. "He stood up and he gave a speech to the crew. We didn’t know necessarily it would be his last day on a set, but he was sort of indicating to us that he thought it was.” Anthony Russo added to the sentiment, calling it a "very emotional" moment. “I think it was in the back of all of our heads, we may never see him on set again… It was clear that he was struggling with his health, and he worked so hard to deliver a performance and a presence." Russo believed the effects of whatever Stewart was going through were hidden by the veteran actor as much as possible, but they sensed something was different about him and appreciated the full effort Stewart delivered. "For him to have muscled through and delivered the performance that he did in that movie, and the experience that he delivered for all of us as collaborators, it made it intensely emotional.”

Rumors about what Marvel Studios will do to honor Stewart's memory have ranged from an "In Memorium" at the conclusion of the film, to a custom opening logo sequence focused on his performances through the years as Professor Xavier. It's a challenge to figure out one way to honor the man when he has given so much to different fandoms over the years. To many, he is their Star Trek captain, and to others he is there Professor X — let alone not forgetting the many other impactful roles Stewart played on stage and screen. One moment will never feel like enough to honor the legend who crossed fandoms and elevated whatever genre he took part in, giving 110% to each role he undertook.

After the news of Stewart's passing broke, tributes from his colleagues poured in . Feige commented on the announcement not long after, writing “It was a true privilege to know him and to work with him. His legacy lives on not only in decades of extraordinary work, but in the many, many people he mentored. He will be deeply missed.” Hugh Jackman wrote "We lost one of the greats of stage and screen today. And, in my book, a tremendous friend and man. I learned so much from him. I will miss you, Patrick Stewart, all of my days.”

How do you hope that Doomsday will honor the memory of Patrick Stewart, and how are you feeling a month after this sad news broke? Let us know in the comments and check in with your fellow grieving fans.
